religion.detail: critic of anthropomorphic gods; one god

nodes.author: hebrew-bible
nodes.context: On the first day of creation, God speaks into the void.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The first act of creation is a sentence: the word or[light] is said before light exists.
nodes.orig: וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר וַיְהִי־אוֹר
nodes.trans: And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
nodes.sourceLabel: Sefaria

nodes.author: hebrew-bible
nodes.context: Having made light, God divides it from darkness and names both.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Naming completes creation: things are not finished until they are called something.
nodes.orig: וַיִּקְרָא אֱלֹהִים לָאוֹר יוֹם וְלַחֹשֶׁךְ קָרָא לָיְלָה
nodes.trans: And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night.
nodes.sourceLabel: Sefaria

nodes.author: hebrew-bible
nodes.context: God brings the animals to Adam to see what he will call each nefesh[living being, soul].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Humanity's first task is naming, and the name Adam gives is the name a thing has.
nodes.orig: וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָא־לוֹ הָאָדָם נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה הוּא שְׁמוֹ
nodes.trans: Whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.
nodes.sourceLabel: Sefaria

nodes.author: homer
nodes.context: Athena appears to Achilles in the quarrel with Agamemnon, and he speaks to her in "winged words."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Homer's most repeated formula: words fly from the speaker like arrows or birds.
nodes.orig: καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα
nodes.trans: And speaking, he addressed her with winged words.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: homer
nodes.context: Nestor rises to calm the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Eloquence as sweetness. Compare the honey-sweet book of Revelation 10:10.
nodes.orig: τοῦ καὶ ἀπὸ γλώσσης μέλιτος γλυκίων ῥέεν αὐδή
nodes.trans: From whose tongue flowed speech sweeter than honey.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: homer
nodes.context: The language of the gods: Thetis recalls summoning the hundred-handed giant to defend Zeus.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Homer several times gives a thing's name in the gods' tongue and in ours: the gods have their own vocabulary.
nodes.orig: ὃν Βριάρεων καλέουσι θεοί, ἄνδρες δέ τε πάντες Αἰγαίων᾽
nodes.trans: Whom the gods call Briareus, but all men Aegaeon.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: homer
nodes.context: The poem opens by asking a goddess to speak through the poet.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Odysseus is polytropos[of many turns], wily in speech as in travel; the epic's hero is a man of words.
nodes.orig: Ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, Μοῦσα, πολύτροπον
nodes.trans: Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: homer
nodes.context: Achilles answers the embassy sent by Agamemnon, refusing to return to battle.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Speech must match the phrēn[heart, mind]: doubleness of word is the worst vice.
nodes.orig: ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσιν / ὅς χ᾽ ἕτερον μὲν κεύθῃ ἐνὶ φρεσίν, ἄλλο δὲ εἴπῃ.
nodes.trans: Hateful to me as the gates of Hades is the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: hebrew-bible
nodes.context: The serpent questions Eve about God's command.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The first temptation is a question about what a sentence meant.
nodes.orig: וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל־הָאִשָּׁה אַף כִּי־אָמַר אֱלֹהִים לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן
nodes.trans: And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?
nodes.sourceLabel: Sefaria

speaker.name: The Serpent
speaker.note: Genesis names only the serpent; Satan is the later Jewish and Christian reading (Wisdom 2:24, Revelation 12:9).

nodes.author: homer
nodes.context: Odysseus to the Cyclops, giving a false name: Outis["Nobody"].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A name becomes a weapon: the West's first word-trick.
nodes.orig: Οὖτις ἐμοί γ᾽ ὄνομα· Οὖτιν δέ με κικλήσκουσι / μήτηρ ἠδὲ πατὴρ ἠδ᾽ ἄλλοι πάντες ἑταῖροι.
nodes.trans: Nobody is my name. Nobody my mother and father call me, and all my companions.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: homer
nodes.context: The blinded Cyclops shouts for help, and his neighbors misread him. Then Odysseus: "how my name and my flawless cunning had fooled them."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The pun runs deeper in Greek: *mē tis* ("no one") sounds like *mētis* ("cunning").
nodes.orig: ὦ φίλοι, Οὖτίς με κτείνει δόλῳ οὐδὲ βίηφιν.
nodes.trans: Friends, Nobody is killing me by trickery, not by force.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: hebrew-bible
nodes.context: At Babel, all people share one safah[lip; language] and build a tower; God goes down to confound it.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A single shared language is treated as power, and its division as the origin of the world's many tongues.
nodes.orig: וַיְהִי כָל־הָאָרֶץ שָׂפָה אֶחָת וּדְבָרִים אֲחָדִים
nodes.trans: And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech…
nodes.sourceLabel: Sefaria

nodes.author: hebrew-bible
nodes.context: A proverb on lashon[tongue; language], from Israel's wisdom literature.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Speech is given the power of life and death.
nodes.orig: מָוֶת וְחַיִּים בְּיַד־לָשׁוֹן
nodes.trans: Death and life are in the power of the tongue.
nodes.sourceLabel: Sefaria

nodes.author: anaximander
nodes.context: The oldest surviving sentence of Western philosophy, quoted by Simplicius, who notes that Anaximander says this "in rather poetic terms."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Cosmic order is put in legal words: dikē[justice; penalty] and tisis[retribution]. Nietzsche (*Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks*, 1873) and Heidegger ("Der Spruch des Anaximander," 1946) both wrote essays on this one sentence.
nodes.orig: ἐξ ὧν δὲ ἡ γένεσίς ἐστι τοῖς οὖσι, καὶ τὴν φθορὰν εἰς ταῦτα γίνεσθαι κατὰ τὸ χρεών· διδόναι γὰρ αὐτὰ δίκην καὶ τίσιν ἀλλήλοις τῆς ἀδικίας κατὰ τὴν τοῦ χρόνου τάξιν.
nodes.trans: From what things have their coming-to-be, into that they also pass away, according to necessity; for they pay penalty and retribution to one another for their injustice, according to the ordering of time.
nodes.sourceLabel: H. Diels, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, griechisch und deutsch (Berlin: Weidmann, 1903), Anaximandros fr. 1 (= DK 12 B1, from Simplicius, In Phys. 24.13)

nodes.author: xenophanes
nodes.context: Xenophanes mocks the human-shaped gods of Homer and Hesiod.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: We make gods in our own image, and name them in our own words.
nodes.orig: ἀλλ᾽ εἰ χεῖρας ἔχον βόες ἵπποι τ᾽ ἠὲ λέοντες / ἢ γράψαι χείρεσσι καὶ ἔργα τελεῖν ἅπερ ἄνδρες, / ἵπποι μέν θ᾽ ἵπποισι, βόες δέ τε βουσὶν ὁμοίας / καί κε θεῶν ἰδέας ἔγραφον…
nodes.trans: If oxen and horses and lions had hands, and could draw and make works as men do, horses would draw the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen…
nodes.relDetail: critic of anthropomorphic gods; one god
nodes.sourceLabel: H. Diels, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker (Berlin: Weidmann, 1903), Xenophanes fr. 15 (Clement, Strom. 5.109.3) and fr. 16 (Clement, Strom. 7.22.1)

nodes.author: hebrew-bible
nodes.context: Isaac's blessing: having blessed Jacob in disguise, Isaac realizes the deception when Esau arrives.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A spoken blessing cannot be taken back.
nodes.orig: גַּם־בָּרוּךְ יִהְיֶה
nodes.trans: Yea, and he shall be blessed.
nodes.sourceLabel: Sefaria

nodes.author: heraclitus
nodes.context: Heraclitus distinguishes his own voice from the Logos it carries.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: *Homologein*[to agree], "to agree," is literally "to say the same logos."
nodes.orig: οὐκ ἐμοῦ, ἀλλὰ τοῦ λόγου ἀκούσαντας ὁμολογεῖν σοφόν ἐστιν ἓν πάντα εἶναι.
nodes.trans: Listening not to me but to the Logos, it is wise to agree that all things are one.
nodes.sourceLabel: H. Diels, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker (Berlin: Weidmann, 1903), Herakleitos fr. 50 (DK 22 B50; from Hippolytus, Refutatio 9.9.1)

nodes.author: heraclitus
nodes.context: The book's opening words.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The Logos[word; reason] holds forever, yet men fail to understand it even after hearing it.
nodes.orig: τοῦ δὲ λόγου τοῦδ᾽ ἐόντος ἀεὶ ἀξύνετοι γίνονται ἄνθρωποι
nodes.trans: Of this Logos, which holds forever, men prove uncomprehending.
nodes.sourceLabel: H. Diels, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker (Berlin: Weidmann, 1903), Herakleitos fr. 1 (DK 22 B1; from Sextus Empiricus, Adv. Math. 7.132)

nodes.author: heraclitus
nodes.context: Heraclitus on the oracle of Apollo at Delphi.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: *Sēmainei*[gives a sign] is the root of "semantics."
nodes.orig: ὁ ἄναξ οὗ τὸ μαντεῖόν ἐστι τὸ ἐν Δελφοῖς οὔτε λέγει οὔτε κρύπτει ἀλλὰ σημαίνει.
nodes.trans: The lord whose oracle is at Delphi neither speaks nor conceals, but gives a sign.
nodes.sourceLabel: H. Diels, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker (Berlin: Weidmann, 1903), Herakleitos fr. 93 (DK 22 B93; from Plutarch, De Pythiae oraculis 404D)

nodes.author: socrates
nodes.context: Socrates left no writings. He is known only through others: Plato's dialogues, Xenophon's memoirs, and Aristophanes' mockery in the Clouds (423 BCE). The three portraits disagree.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The founder of Western philosophy is a character in other people's books. Separating the historical man from Plato's spokesman is the "Socratic problem": the critic of writing survives only as writing, and the speaker behind the text cannot be recovered.
nodes.sourceLabel: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Socrates"

nodes.author: hebrew-bible
nodes.context: Jacob wrestles through the night and is renamed at dawn (32:29 in Hebrew numbering).
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A new name marks a new identity: the struggle ends in a word.
nodes.orig: לֹא יַעֲקֹב יֵאָמֵר עוֹד שִׁמְךָ כִּי אִם־יִשְׂרָאֵל
nodes.trans: Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel.
nodes.sourceLabel: Sefaria

nodes.author: thucydides
nodes.context: Pericles' Funeral Oration praises Athenian democracy.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Athens defines itself as a city that talks before it acts: logos[word] with ergon[deed].
nodes.orig: οὐ τοὺς λόγους τοῖς ἔργοις βλάβην ἡγούμενοι
nodes.trans: We do not think that words are a hindrance to deeds.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: thucydides
nodes.context: In his statement of method, Thucydides explains how he rendered the speeches in his history.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Thucydides admits his famous speeches are reconstructions.
nodes.orig: ὡς δ᾽ ἂν ἐδόκουν μοι ἕκαστοι περὶ τῶν αἰεὶ παρόντων τὰ δέοντα μάλιστ᾽ εἰπεῖν
nodes.trans: As it seemed to me each speaker would most likely have said what the occasion required.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: gorgias
nodes.context: Gorgias defends Helen: if speech persuaded her, she is not to blame.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Speech is a dynastēs[lord, ruler]. Gorgias goes on to compare speech's effect on the soul to a drug's effect on the body.
nodes.orig: λόγος δυνάστης μέγας ἐστίν, ὃς σμικροτάτῳ σώματι καὶ ἀφανεστάτῳ θειότατα ἔργα ἀποτελεῖ.
nodes.trans: Speech is a mighty lord, who with the smallest and most invisible body accomplishes the most divine works.
nodes.sourceLabel: Greek, Perseus

nodes.author: thucydides
nodes.context: Thucydides explains why his history may seem less pleasing to listeners.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Writing set against oral performance: a ktēma[possession] for all time, not an agōnisma[prize-piece].
nodes.orig: κτῆμά τε ἐς αἰεὶ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀγώνισμα ἐς τὸ παραχρῆμα ἀκούειν ξύγκειται.
nodes.trans: It is composed as a possession for all time, rather than a prize-piece to be heard for the moment.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: hebrew-bible
nodes.context: Near the end of Ecclesiastes, the Preacher warns his son against more study.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: An ancient weariness with the endless multiplication of written words.
nodes.orig: עֲשׂוֹת סְפָרִים הַרְבֵּה אֵין קֵץ
nodes.trans: Of making many books there is no end.
nodes.sourceLabel: Sefaria

nodes.author: thucydides
nodes.context: During the civil war in Corcyra, Thucydides describes how faction corrupted the city.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: When politics breaks down, the meanings of words shift first.
nodes.orig: καὶ τὴν εἰωθυῖαν ἀξίωσιν τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐς τὰ ἔργα ἀντήλλαξαν τῇ δικαιώσει. τόλμα μὲν γὰρ ἀλόγιστος ἀνδρεία φιλέταιρος ἐνομίσθη, μέλλησις δὲ προμηθὴς δειλία εὐπρεπής, τὸ δὲ σῶφρον τοῦ ἀνάνδρου πρόσχημα.
nodes.trans: They changed the customary meaning of words in relation to deeds, as they saw fit. Reckless daring came to be considered loyal courage; prudent hesitation, specious cowardice; moderation, a cloak for unmanliness.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: panini
nodes.context: A meta-rule explaining how the marker consonants of the Śiva Sūtras are used: so aC means "every vowel" and haL "every consonant."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: This is a character class, defined by a rule of the grammar about the grammar.
nodes.orig: आदिरन्त्येन सहेता
nodes.trans: An initial (sound), together with a final marker, (names the whole range between).
nodes.sourceLabel: Text and commentary, ashtadhyayi.com

nodes.author: panini
nodes.context: The first of fourteen lines, in the phonemic catalogue that precedes the Aṣṭādhyāyī[Pāṇini's grammar], that list every sound of Sanskrit.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Each line ends in a silent marker consonant (here ṇ) that is never pronounced. The markers exist only so that later rules can name ranges of the list.
nodes.orig: अइउण्
nodes.trans: a i u ṇ.
nodes.sourceLabel: Text and commentary, ashtadhyayi.com

nodes.author: plato
nodes.context: Hermogenes reports Cratylus' thesis, which Socrates spends the dialogue testing against Hermogenes' view that names are mere convention.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Are names correct by physis[nature] or by agreement? The founding question of the philosophy of language.
nodes.orig: ὀνόματος ὀρθότητα εἶναι ἑκάστῳ τῶν ὄντων φύσει πεφυκυῖαν
nodes.trans: There is a correctness of name for each thing, belonging to it by nature.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: plato
nodes.context: King Thamus answers the god Theuth, who offers writing as a gift to Egypt.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Derrida's essay "Plato's Pharmacy" (1968) is built on the word *pharmakon*[remedy and poison], which means both remedy and poison.
nodes.orig: τοῦτο γὰρ τῶν μαθόντων λήθην μὲν ἐν ψυχαῖς παρέξει μνήμης ἀμελετησίᾳ… οὔκουν μνήμης ἀλλὰ ὑπομνήσεως φάρμακον ηὗρες.
nodes.trans: This will produce forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn it, through neglect of memory… You have found a drug not for memory but for reminding.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: plato
nodes.context: Socrates continues his critique of writing after the myth of Theuth.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Written words are like paintings: "if you ask them something, they keep a most solemn silence."
nodes.orig: ἐὰν δ᾽ ἀνέρῃ τι, σεμνῶς πάνυ σιγᾷ.
nodes.trans: if you ask them something, they keep a most solemn silence.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: panini
nodes.context: The first rule. The grammar opens not with a statement about Sanskrit but with a definition of its own technical vocabulary.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Vṛddhi means "growth," and the first word of the work is chosen as an auspicious one.
nodes.orig: वृद्धिरादैच्
nodes.trans: Vṛddhi[strongest vowel grade] (is the name for) ā, ai, au.
nodes.sourceLabel: Text and commentary, ashtadhyayi.com

nodes.author: plato
nodes.context: Socrates finishes his complaint against written words: once written, a text drifts everywhere, reaching those who understand it and those who don't.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A text cannot defend itself or answer questions; without its author it is an orphan. Every documentation problem since.
nodes.orig: τοῦ πατρὸς ἀεὶ δεῖται βοηθοῦ
nodes.trans: it always needs its father to help it
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: plato
nodes.context: Socrates describes a better kind of word, one written in the soul of the learner, and Phaedrus names it.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The written word is an eidōlon[image, phantom] of the living one. The paradox, which Derrida exploits, is that Plato makes the case in writing, and the only Socrates we have is a written one. Naur's "theory" that lives in programmers rather than in code is the same claim.
nodes.orig: τὸν τοῦ εἰδότος λόγον λέγεις ζῶντα καὶ ἔμψυχον, οὗ ὁ γεγραμμένος εἴδωλον ἄν τι λέγοιτο δικαίως.
nodes.trans: You mean the living and ensouled word of the one who knows, of which the written word might fairly be called an image.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: plato
nodes.context: Plato rebukes those who have written about his teachings on the highest mathēma[subject of study].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Plato's own Tractatus[Wittgenstein's treatise] 7: what matters most cannot be said.
nodes.orig: ῥητὸν γὰρ οὐδαμῶς ἐστιν ὡς ἄλλα μαθήματα… ἐξαίφνης, οἷον ἀπὸ πυρὸς πηδήσαντος ἐξαφθὲν φῶς, ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ γενόμενον
nodes.trans: It cannot be put into words like other studies… but suddenly, like light kindled from a leaping spark, it is born in the soul.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: aristotle
nodes.context: Aristotle opens his treatise on propositions by defining spoken and written words.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The foundation of Western semantics for two thousand years: words as symbola[tokens, signs] of pathēmata[affections] in the soul.
nodes.orig: Ἔστι μὲν οὖν τὰ ἐν τῇ φωνῇ τῶν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ παθημάτων σύμβολα, καὶ τὰ γραφόμενα τῶν ἐν τῇ φωνῇ.
nodes.trans: Spoken sounds are symbols of affections in the soul, and written marks are symbols of spoken sounds.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: aristotle
nodes.context: Aristotle defines the onoma[name, noun] at the start of his analysis.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Aristotle's answer to the *Cratylus*: names hold by synthēkē[convention].
nodes.orig: Ὄνομα μὲν οὖν ἐστὶ φωνὴ σημαντικὴ κατὰ συνθήκην
nodes.trans: A name is a sound significant by convention.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: panini
nodes.context: A rule telling the reader how to read words cited inside the grammar's own rules.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: This is the distinction between using a word and mentioning it, stated about 2,300 years before logicians named it.
nodes.orig: स्वं रूपं शब्दस्याशब्दसंज्ञा
nodes.trans: A word (in a rule) stands for its own form, except when it is a technical term.
nodes.sourceLabel: Text and commentary, ashtadhyayi.com

nodes.author: panini
nodes.context: A precedence rule for the grammar's own rules.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The commentators spent two millennia arguing about what "later" means.
nodes.orig: विप्रतिषेधे परं कार्यम्
nodes.trans: When (two rules) conflict, the later one applies.
nodes.sourceLabel: Text and commentary, ashtadhyayi.com

nodes.author: mahabharata
nodes.context: Krishna describes the imperishable and the dying man's utterance of Om.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The same word names the indestructible and the written letter.
nodes.orig: अक्षरं ब्रह्म परमं / ओमित्येकाक्षरं ब्रह्म व्याहरन्मामनुस्मरन्
nodes.trans: Brahman[ultimate reality] is the supreme imperishable (akṣara[letter; imperishable])… Uttering Om, the one-syllable (eka-akṣara) Brahman, and remembering me…
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885), Gutenberg

nodes.author: mahabharata
nodes.context: Krishna lists his manifestations, the best of each kind.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: God names himself as a syllable.
nodes.orig: गिरामस्म्येकमक्षरम्
nodes.trans: Of utterances, I am the single syllable.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885), Gutenberg

nodes.author: lucretius
nodes.context: Lucretius argues that nothing comes from nothing and that things share atoms.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: *Elementa*[letters; atoms] means both "letters" and "atoms": the universe is spelled. He returns to the analogy at 1.823–827 and 2.688–699.
nodes.orig: ut potius multis communia corpora rebus / multa putes esse, ut verbis elementa videmus, / quam sine principiis ullam rem exsistere posse.
nodes.trans: Rather believe that many bodies are common to many things, as we see letters common to words, than that anything can exist without first-beginnings.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Leonard 1916

nodes.author: lucretius
nodes.context: In his history of civilization, Lucretius turns to the origin of language.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Language arose from nature and utilitas[usefulness, need], not invention.
nodes.orig: at varios linguae sonitus natura subegit / mittere et utilitas expressit nomina rerum.
nodes.trans: But nature drove men to utter the various sounds of the tongue, and usefulness pressed out the names of things.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Leonard 1916

nodes.author: lucretius
nodes.context: Lucretius continues his account of how language arose.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A direct rejection of a single original name-giver, whether Adam in Genesis 2:19 or the lawgiver of the *Cratylus*.
nodes.orig: proinde putare aliquem tum nomina distribuisse / rebus et inde homines didicisse vocabula prima, / desiperest.
nodes.trans: To think that someone back then handed out names to things, and that men learned their first words from him, is madness.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Leonard 1916

nodes.author: caesar
nodes.context: Caesar describes the Druids of Gaul, whose pupils spend up to twenty years memorizing verse. The Druids use Greek letters for everyday records but refuse to write their teachings down, for two reasons: so the doctrine does not reach the common people, and so learners do not neglect memory.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Plato's warning about writing, observed in a living oral culture three centuries later, and combined with a second motive, secrecy. Writing both spreads knowledge and weakens the memory that held it.
nodes.orig: …quod fere plerisque accidit ut praesidio litterarum diligentiam in perdiscendo ac memoriam remittant.
nodes.trans: …which happens to most people: trusting to the protection of letters, they relax their effort in learning and their memory.
nodes.sourceLabel: The Latin Library

nodes.author: horace
nodes.context: Horace advises a young friend on discretion with powerful patrons.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A spoken word cannot be unsaid.
nodes.orig: et semel emissum volat irrevocabile verbum.
nodes.trans: And a word once let out flies, beyond recall.
nodes.sourceLabel: Horace, Epistulae 1.18.71 (The Latin Library text)

nodes.author: mahabharata
nodes.context: The dvandva is the copulative compound ("this-and-that").
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Krishna identifies himself with the first letter, as the God of Revelation calls himself Alpha, and also with a category of Sanskrit grammar.
nodes.orig: अक्षराणामकारोऽस्मि द्वन्द्वः सामासिकस्य च
nodes.trans: Of letters I am the letter A, and of compounds the dvandva[copulative compound].
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885), Gutenberg

nodes.author: horace
nodes.context: Horace advises a young poet on choosing words.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Novelty lies in the iunctura[joining of words], not in new words.
nodes.orig: dixeris egregie, notum si callida verbum / reddiderit iunctura novum.
nodes.trans: You will speak exceptionally well if a clever combination makes a familiar word new.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: horace
nodes.context: Horace on how vocabulary rises and falls over time.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Two millennia before Wittgenstein, usus[usage] is the authority.
nodes.orig: multa renascentur quae iam cecidere, cadentque / quae nunc sunt in honore vocabula, si volet usus, / quem penes arbitrium est et ius et norma loquendi.
nodes.trans: Many words now fallen will be reborn, and many now honored will fall, if usage wills it, in whose hands lie the judgment, the law, and the rule of speaking.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: horace
nodes.context: Horace advises keeping a poem nine years before publishing.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Publication is irreversible: a word sent out cannot be recalled.
nodes.orig: delere licebit / quod non edideris; nescit vox missa reverti.
nodes.trans: What you have not published you may destroy; the word once sent forth cannot return.
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus

nodes.author: mahabharata
nodes.context: Krishna on those who recite the Vedic rituals for reward.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A warning against those who love the letter of the Veda.
nodes.orig: यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः
nodes.trans: This flowery speech that the undiscerning proclaim…
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885), Gutenberg

nodes.author: paul-of-tarsus
nodes.context: Paul's hymn to love contrasts present partial knowledge with future full knowledge.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: "Darkly" is *en ainigmati*, literally "in a riddle." Source of Philip K. Dick's title *A Scanner Darkly*.
nodes.orig: βλέπομεν γὰρ ἄρτι δι᾽ ἐσόπτρου ἐν αἰνίγματι, τότε δὲ πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον.
nodes.trans: For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: paul-of-tarsus
nodes.context: Paul contrasts the old covenant written on stone with the new written on hearts.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The gramma[written letter] kills, the pneuma[spirit; breath] gives life: the founding text against literal reading.
nodes.orig: τὸ γὰρ γράμμα ἀποκτέννει, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ζῳοποιεῖ.
nodes.trans: For the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: new-testament
nodes.context: James warns teachers and believers about the dangers of the unbridled tongue.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A small organ that can set a whole life ablaze: speech as fire.
nodes.orig: καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα πῦρ
nodes.trans: And the tongue is a fire.
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: mahabharata
nodes.context: On austerity of speech.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Such speech is listed as a discipline, vāṅmayaṃ tapaḥ[austerity of speech].
nodes.orig: अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत्
nodes.trans: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial…
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885), Gutenberg

nodes.author: new-testament
nodes.context: At the start of Revelation, God speaks in his own voice.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: God names himself by the first and last letters of the alphabet.
nodes.orig: Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ
nodes.trans: I am Alpha and Omega.
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: new-testament
nodes.context: To the church at Pergamum, the one who overcomes is promised a white psēphos[pebble; voting stone] with a secret name.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A word with exactly one speaker.
nodes.orig: καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ψῆφον ὄνομα καινὸν γεγραμμένον ὃ οὐδεὶς οἶδεν εἰ μὴ ὁ λαμβάνων
nodes.trans: And in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: new-testament
nodes.context: John is about to write down what the seven thunders said, and a voice from heaven stops him.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Revelation's own Tractatus[Wittgenstein's treatise] 7, whose last proposition enjoins silence.
nodes.orig: Σφράγισον ἃ ἐλάλησαν αἱ ἑπτὰ βρονταί, καὶ μὴ αὐτὰ γράψῃς.
nodes.trans: Seal up those things which the seven thunders uttered, and write them not.
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: new-testament
nodes.context: An angel gives John a little book and tells him to eat it. John eats the book.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The word must be ingested before it can be prophesied, sweet to speak and bitter to digest.
nodes.orig: καὶ ἦν ἐν τῷ στόματί μου ὡς μέλι γλυκύ, καὶ ὅτε ἔφαγον αὐτό, ἐπικράνθη ἡ κοιλία μου.
nodes.trans: It was in my mouth sweet as honey: and as soon as I had eaten it, my belly was bitter.
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: new-testament
nodes.context: A rider on a white horse appears, his robe dipped in blood.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: John 1:1's Logos[word; reason] returns at the end.
nodes.orig: καὶ κέκληται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ.
nodes.trans: And his name is called The Word of God.
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: new-testament
nodes.context: The opening of John's Gospel echoes Genesis 1:1, recasting creation through the Word.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: *Logos*[word; reason] also means reason, account, and ratio.
nodes.orig: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
nodes.trans: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: new-testament
nodes.context: The last verses of the last book warn every reader and copyist.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The Bible ends with a warning about editing.
nodes.orig: ἐάν τις ἐπιθῇ ἐπ᾽ αὐτά… καὶ ἐάν τις ἀφέλῃ ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων τοῦ βιβλίου…
nodes.trans: If any man shall add unto these things… and if any man shall take away from the words of the book…
nodes.sourceLabel: Interlinear

nodes.author: mahabharata
nodes.context: Krishna's words in his universal form.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Oppenheimer's rendering of this line is in the mid-twentieth-century section.
nodes.orig: कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो
nodes.trans: I am Time (kāla[time; death]), grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885), Gutenberg

nodes.author: augustine
nodes.context: Augustine opens his treatise on signs, written to teach the reading of Scripture.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The West's working definition of a sign for a thousand years.
nodes.orig: Signum est enim res, praeter speciem quam ingerit sensibus, aliud aliquid ex se faciens in cogitationem venire.
nodes.trans: A sign is a thing which, beyond the impression it makes on the senses, causes something else to come into the mind.
nodes.sourceLabel: Augustine, De doctrina christiana II.1.1 (Latin text, augustinus.it, from PL 34)

nodes.author: augustine
nodes.context: Augustine recalls how he learned to speak as a child.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Wittgenstein opens the Philosophical Investigations with this passage.
nodes.orig: cum ipsi appellabant rem aliquam et cum secundum eam vocem corpus ad aliquid movebant, videbam et tenebam hoc ab eis vocari rem illam, quod sonabant, cum eam vellent ostendere.
nodes.trans: When grown-ups named some object and moved their bodies toward it as they spoke, I saw this and grasped that the thing was called by the sound they made when they meant to point it out.
nodes.sourceLabel: Latin, ed. O'Donnell

nodes.author: boethius
nodes.context: Written in prison awaiting execution. Boethius describes Lady Philosophy's robe.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Pi for praktikē[practical philosophy] (practical philosophy), theta for theōrētikē[theoretical philosophy] (theoretical). Philosophy literally wears letters.
nodes.orig: Harum in extrema margine Π Graecum, in supremo vero Θ legebatur intextum.
nodes.trans: On its lowest hem was woven the Greek letter Π, and on the highest, Θ.
nodes.sourceLabel: Latin & English, Loeb 1918

nodes.author: boethius
nodes.context: Lady Philosophy cites Plato (From Timaeus 29b).
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words must fit their objects: Plato's principle, passed to the Middle Ages through Boethius.
nodes.orig: Platone sanciente didicisti cognatos de quibus loquuntur rebus oportere esse sermones.
nodes.trans: You have learned on Plato's authority that words must be akin to the things of which they speak.
nodes.sourceLabel: Latin & English, Loeb 1918

nodes.author: beowulf-poet
nodes.context: The opening lines of the poem.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The poem begins by citing what has been told.
nodes.orig: Hwæt! We Gardena in geardagum, / þeodcyninga, þrym gefrunon
nodes.trans: Listen! We have heard of the glory of the Spear-Danes' kings in days of old.
nodes.sourceLabel: Old English with facing translation, ed. Slade

nodes.author: al-khwarizmi
nodes.work: al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala
nodes.context: Al-Jabr[restoration], the setting of broken bones, became "algebra," and the Latin form of his name, Algoritmi, became "algorithm." His algebra contains no symbols: everything is written in sentences, with the unknown called shayʾ ("thing"), its square māl ("wealth"), and constants dirham[silver coin].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The popular claim that shayʾ became our x is unproven.
nodes.orig: الكتاب المختصر في حساب الجبر والمقابلة
nodes.trans: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Restoration and Balancing.
nodes.sourceLabel: F. Rosen (ed. and trans.), The Algebra of Mohammed ben Musa (London: Oriental Translation Fund, 1831), Arabic text and English

nodes.author: al-kindi
nodes.context: Al-Kindī defends using Greek learning in Arabic: we should not be ashamed to recognize truth and take it from wherever it comes, even from distant races and foreign nations, for nothing is more fitting for a seeker of truth than truth itself.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The founding argument for translation as a philosophical duty.
nodes.sourceLabel: Alfred L. Ivry, Al-Kindi's Metaphysics: A Translation of Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi's Treatise 'On First Philosophy' (Albany: SUNY Press, 1974)

nodes.author: beowulf-poet
nodes.context: The scop's[court poet's] song in Heorot[Danish king's hall]: Genesis, sung inside a pagan hall.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: This song is what enrages Grendel.
nodes.orig: Þær wæs hearpan sweg, / swutol sang scopes. Sægde se þe cuþe / frumsceaft fira feorran reccan, / cwæð þæt se Ælmihtiga eorðan worhte
nodes.trans: There was the sound of the harp, the clear song of the poet. He who knew how to tell of the origin of men from far back said that the Almighty made the earth.
nodes.sourceLabel: Old English, ed. Slade

nodes.author: alfred
nodes.authorName: Alfred the Great and his circle
nodes.context: The Anglo-Saxon translator of Boethius introduces a speech of Lady Philosophy.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: He gives Lady Philosophy the same formula as Beowulf.
nodes.orig: Ða se wisdom eft wordhord onleac
nodes.trans: Then Wisdom again unlocked her word-hoard[store of words].
nodes.sourceLabel: W. J. Sedgefield (ed.), King Alfred's Old English Version of Boethius De consolatione philosophiae (Oxford: Clarendon, 1899), Metre 6, line 1

nodes.author: al-sirafi
nodes.work: debate with Abū Bishr Mattā ibn Yūnus
nodes.context: The grammarian al-Sīrāfī attacks the logician Mattā: Aristotle's logic, he argues, is Greek grammar in disguise, and no one can reason correctly in Arabic without mastering Arabic itself.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The first recorded debate on whether logic is universal or tied to a particular language, a thousand years before Wittgenstein.
nodes.sourceLabel: Abū Ḥayyān al-Tawḥīdī, Kitāb al-Imtāʿ wa-l-muʾānasa, Night 8; English: D. S. Margoliouth, 'The Discussion between Abu Bishr Matta and Abu Sa'id al-Sirafi on the Merits of Logic and Grammar', JRAS 1905

nodes.author: al-farabi
nodes.work: Iḥṣāʾ al-ʿulūm (Enumeration of the Sciences); Kitāb al-Ḥurūf (Book of Letters)
nodes.context: Al-Fārābī answers al-Sīrāfī: logic stands to the intellect as grammar stands to language, giving rules common to all languages where grammar gives the rules of one.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The Book of Letters tells how a people's language grows from first gestures and sounds into poetry, rhetoric, and finally philosophy.
nodes.sourceLabel: al-Fārābī, Kitāb al-Ḥurūf (Book of Letters); Iḥṣāʾ al-ʿulūm

nodes.author: beowulf-poet
nodes.context: Beowulf, leading his men, answers the Danish coast-guard.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words as a guarded treasure.
nodes.orig: Him se yldesta ondswarode, / werodes wisa, wordhord onleac
nodes.trans: The eldest answered him, the leader of the troop, unlocked his word-hoard[store of words].
nodes.sourceLabel: Perseus, line 259

nodes.author: omar-khayyam
nodes.context: Khayyām solved cubic equations geometrically in his Treatise on the Demonstration of Problems of Algebra (c. 1070) and is credited with the Rubāʿiyyāt[quatrains], though many quatrains are of uncertain authorship. Edward FitzGerald's loose English version (1859, stanza 51 of the first edition).
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Horace's nescit vox missa reverti[speech cannot return], turned into fate. I have not confirmed which Persian quatrain FitzGerald adapted.
nodes.orig: The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, / Moves on: nor all thy Piety nor Wit / Shall lure it back to cancel half a Line, / Nor all thy Tears wash out a Word of it.
nodes.sourceLabel: FitzGerald, Rubáiyát, Gutenberg

nodes.author: aquinas
nodes.context: The question is whether God can be named at all.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Wittgenstein owned a German–Latin edition of these first questions of the Summa at his death.
nodes.orig: secundum Philosophum, voces sunt signa intellectuum, et intellectus sunt rerum similitudines.
nodes.trans: According to the Philosopher, words are signs of concepts, and concepts are likenesses of things.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, CCEL

nodes.author: aquinas
nodes.context: Aquinas asks whether Scripture can have several senses.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: For Aquinas, the world is also a text.
nodes.orig: auctor sacrae Scripturae est Deus, in cuius potestate est ut non solum voces ad significandum accommodet (quod etiam homo facere potest), sed etiam res ipsas.
nodes.trans: The author of Holy Scripture is God, in whose power it is to make not only words signify (which a man can also do) but things themselves.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, CCEL

nodes.author: rumi
nodes.context: The opening lines of the Masnavī[rhyming-couplet poem]; Rūmī is a poet, not a mathematician. The reed flute speaks because it was cut from its reed-bed.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: On this reading, all speech is a lament for lost unity, a Persian Babel.
nodes.orig: بشنو این نی چون شکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها حکایت می‌کند
nodes.trans: Listen to this reed, how it complains, telling a tale of separations.
nodes.sourceLabel: Rūmī, Masnavī-yi maʿnavī, Daftar I, verse 1 (Ganjoor text)

nodes.author: aquinas
nodes.context: After an experience at Mass, Aquinas stopped writing and left the Summa unfinished.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The medieval Tractatus 7.
nodes.orig: Omnia quae scripsi videntur mihi paleae.
nodes.trans: Everything I have written seems to me like straw.
nodes.sourceLabel: Testimony of Bartholomew of Capua, Naples canonization inquiry (1319), in Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis

nodes.author: latin-proverb
nodes.context: A medieval Latin proverb, often attributed to a speech in the Roman Senate.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Speech is fleeting, writing endures; the line has been read as both praise and warning.
nodes.orig: Verba volant, scripta manent.
nodes.trans: Spoken words fly away; written ones remain.
nodes.sourceLabel: Latin proverb (medieval; anonymous, sometimes traced without evidence to a speech by Caius Titus in the Roman Senate)

nodes.author: ibn-khaldun
nodes.context: Language, Ibn Khaldūn argues, is a malaka[acquired habit], a habit acquired by practice like a craft, not a set of rules.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Grammar is knowledge about the habit, and one can know the grammar without having the habit.
nodes.sourceLabel: Ibn Khaldūn, al-Muqaddima; English trans. Franz Rosenthal, The Muqaddimah (Princeton UP, 1958), online text

nodes.author: machiavelli
nodes.context: Machiavelli on how a new religion erases the old.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Machiavelli adds that Christianity could not wholly erase pagan memory only because it had to write its new law in Latin, the old enemy's tongue. Memory survives in the grammar the victors were forced to keep.
nodes.orig: Perché quando e' surge una setta nuova, cioè una religione nuova, il primo studio suo è, per darsi riputazione, estinguere la vecchia; e, quando gli occorre che gli ordinatori della nuova setta siano di lingua diversa, la spengono facilmente.
nodes.trans: For when a new sect arises, that is, a new religion, its first concern, to make a name for itself, is to extinguish the old one; and when the founders of the new sect happen to speak a different language, they extinguish it easily.
nodes.sourceLabel: Italian, Wikisource

nodes.author: machiavelli
nodes.work: Discorsi sopra la prima deca di Tito Livio
nodes.context: Machiavelli explains why so little is remembered of the world before Rome.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Language change ranks with flood and plague as a destroyer of memory.
nodes.orig: Che la variazione delle sette e delle lingue, insieme con l'accidente de' diluvii o della peste, spegne le memorie delle cose.
nodes.trans: That the changing of religions and of languages, together with the accident of floods or plague, extinguishes the memory of things.
nodes.sourceLabel: Italian, Wikisource

nodes.author: machiavelli
nodes.context: His example: when Rome expelled its kings, it kept a priest called the *Rex Sacrificulus*[king of sacrifices], "king of the sacrifices," so the people would not miss the word "king."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The name outlives the thing.
nodes.orig: Colui che desidera o che vuole riformare uno stato d'una città, a volere che sia accetto, e poterlo con satisfazione di ciascuno mantenere, è necessitato a ritenere l'ombra almanco de' modi antichi, acciò che a' popoli non paia avere mutato ordine, ancora che in fatto gli ordini nuovi fussero al tutto alieni dai passati.
nodes.trans: Whoever wishes to reform the government of a city, and have it accepted and maintained to everyone's satisfaction, must keep at least the shadow of the ancient forms, so that the people do not seem to have changed their order, even though in fact the new orders are wholly foreign to the old.
nodes.sourceLabel: Italian, Wikisource

nodes.author: montaigne
nodes.context: In "Of Glory," Montaigne asks what fame actually attaches to.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The name is outside the thing: glory clings only to a sound.
nodes.orig: Il y a le nom et la chose: le nom, c'est une voix qui remerque et signifie la chose; le nom, ce n'est pas une partie de la chose ny de la substance, c'est une piece estrangere joincte à la chose, et hors d'elle.
nodes.trans: There is the name and the thing. The name is a sound that marks and signifies the thing; the name is no part of the thing or of its substance; it is a foreign piece attached to the thing, and outside it.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Cotton translation, Gutenberg

nodes.author: montaigne
nodes.context: In "Of Experience," his last essay, Montaigne reflects on conversation.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Meaning is shared between speaker and listener.
nodes.orig: La parole est moitié à celuy qui parle, moitié à celuy qui l'escoute.
nodes.trans: Speech belongs half to the one who speaks, half to the one who listens.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Cotton translation, Gutenberg

nodes.author: shakespeare
nodes.context: Juliet, on her balcony, wishes Romeo had another family name.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The *Cratylus*[Plato's dialogue] question, asked on a balcony.
nodes.orig: What's in a name? That which we call a rose / By any other word would smell as sweet.
nodes.sourceLabel: Folger

nodes.author: shakespeare
nodes.context: Hamlet mocks Polonius while pretending madness; later Claudius fails to pray.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words emptied of thought, twice: once as a joke, once as a damnation.
nodes.orig: POLONIUS: What do you read, my lord? / HAMLET: Words, words, words.
nodes.sourceLabel: Folger

nodes.author: shakespeare
nodes.context: Caliban answers Prospero and Miranda, who taught him their language.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Language as the colonizer's gift and weapon, turned back against him.
nodes.orig: CALIBAN: You taught me language, and my profit on 't / Is I know how to curse. The red plague rid you / For learning me your language!
nodes.sourceLabel: Folger

nodes.author: bacon
nodes.context: Bacon lists four kinds of idols that distort the mind; the third are the Idols of the Marketplace.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words do not just serve reason; they bend it.
nodes.orig: At Idola Fori omnium molestissima sunt, quae ex foedere verborum et nominum se insinuarunt in intellectum. Credunt enim homines rationem suam verbis imperare; sed fit etiam ut verba vim suam super intellectum retorqueant et reflectant.
nodes.trans: But the Idols of the Marketplace are the most troublesome of all: they have crept into the understanding through the alliance of words and names. For men believe that their reason governs words; but it also happens that words turn back and reflect their power upon the understanding.
nodes.sourceLabel: Latin, The Latin Library

nodes.author: descartes
nodes.context: Of machines built to look like us: Descartes adds that even the dullest human can arrange words into speech, while no animal can.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: This is the ancestor of the Turing test and of *Blade Runner*'s Voigt-Kampff[replicant test] interview.
nodes.orig: …jamais elles ne pourraient user de paroles, ni d'autres signes en les composant, comme nous faisons pour déclarer aux autres nos pensées.
nodes.trans: …they could never use words, or other signs, by composing them as we do to declare our thoughts to others.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Gutenberg

nodes.author: hobbes
nodes.context: Hobbes opens his chapter "Of Speech."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: For Hobbes, the social contract is first of all a contract in words.
nodes.orig: But the most noble and profitable invention of all other, was that of SPEECH… without which, there had been amongst men, neither Common-wealth, nor Society, nor Contract, nor Peace, no more than amongst Lyons, Bears, and Wolves.
nodes.sourceLabel: Gutenberg

nodes.author: hobbes
nodes.context: Hobbes on the need for exact definitions.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The wise use words as tokens for counting; fools mistake them for real money.
nodes.orig: For words are wise mens counters, they do but reckon by them: but they are the mony of fooles.
nodes.sourceLabel: Gutenberg

nodes.author: pascal
nodes.context: A fragment from Pascal's unfinished notes for a defense of Christianity.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Meaning lives in arrangement, not in the words alone.
nodes.orig: Les mots diversement rangés font un divers sens, et les sens diversement rangés font différents effets.
nodes.trans: Words differently arranged have a different meaning, and meanings differently arranged have different effects.
nodes.sourceLabel: Pascal, Pensées, Brunschvicg 23 / Lafuma 784 (édition électronique, penseesdepascal.fr)

nodes.author: pascal
nodes.context: Pascal answers critics who say he has nothing new to say.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The anthologist's creed.
nodes.orig: Qu'on ne dise pas que je n'ai rien dit de nouveau ; la disposition des matières est nouvelle.
nodes.trans: Let no one say I have said nothing new: the arrangement of the material is new.
nodes.sourceLabel: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, in Œuvres complètes, Hachette 1871, vol. 1, Pensées, Article VII (Brunschvicg 22 / Lafuma 696); Wikisource

nodes.author: locke
nodes.context: Locke opens Book III, "Of Words," with the signification of words.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words point to ideas in a mind, not to things in the world.
nodes.orig: Words, in their primary or immediate signification, stand for nothing but the ideas in the mind of him that uses them.
nodes.sourceLabel: Gutenberg, Vol. 2 (Books III–IV)

nodes.author: locke
nodes.context: Book III, "Of Words," ends with chapters on the "imperfection" and "abuse" of words; here Locke sums up their danger.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words as a fogged lens between mind and world.
nodes.orig: …they interpose themselves so much between our understandings and the truth… that, like the medium through which visible objects pass, their obscurity and disorder do not seldom cast a mist before our eyes.
nodes.sourceLabel: Gutenberg, Vol. 2

nodes.author: nagesha
nodes.context: A maxim of the grammarians. Often attributed to Patañjali, but the source usually cited is Nāgeśa's collection of interpretive maxims.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The tradition's own joke about its love of brevity.
nodes.orig: अर्धमात्रालाघवेन पुत्रोत्सवं मन्यन्ते वैयाकरणाः
nodes.trans: Grammarians rejoice over saving half a mora[syllable length unit] as over the birth of a son.
nodes.sourceLabel: Nāgojībhaṭṭa, Paribhāṣenduśekhara, ed. and trans. F. Kielhorn (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1868-74)

nodes.author: rousseau
nodes.context: Rousseau argues that the first languages were sung and figurative.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Metaphor before literal meaning; Derrida's *Of Grammatology*[science of writing] devotes a long section to this essay.
nodes.orig: Que la première invention de la parole ne vient pas des besoins, mais des passions… Le langage figuré fut le premier à naître.
nodes.trans: That the first invention of speech came not from needs but from passions… Figurative language was the first to be born.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, with Herder, U. of Chicago Press

nodes.author: johnson
nodes.work: A Dictionary of the English Language
nodes.context: In the Preface to his Dictionary, Johnson reflects on the limits of lexicography[dictionary making].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words are mortal signs; the dictionary-maker wishes they could be fixed.
nodes.orig: I am not yet so lost in lexicography, as to forget that words are the daughters of earth, and that things are the sons of heaven. Language is only the instrument of science, and words are but the signs of ideas: I wish, however, that the instrument might be less apt to decay, and that signs might be permanent, like the things which they denote.
nodes.sourceLabel: Gutenberg

nodes.author: rousseau
nodes.context: In his chapter on writing, Rousseau traces scripts from pictures to signs for words to the alphabet, and asks what writing does to the spoken language it records.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Recording is not neutral: a language written down becomes a different language, precise and cold. This is the passage Derrida's Of Grammatology takes apart.
nodes.orig: L'écriture, qui semble devoir fixer la langue, est précisément ce qui l'altère; elle n'en change pas les mots, mais le génie; elle substitue l'exactitude à l'expression.
nodes.trans: Writing, which seems meant to fix language, is precisely what alters it; it changes not its words but its genius; it substitutes exactness for expression.
nodes.sourceLabel: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Essai sur l'origine des langues, ch. V « De l'Écriture » (posthumous, 1781); Wikisource

nodes.author: herder
nodes.work: Abhandlung über den Ursprung der Sprache
nodes.context: Herder's prize essay for the Berlin Academy, published in the same English volume as Rousseau's.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Language is not a divine gift or a later invention but part of human nature from the start.
nodes.orig: Schon als Tier hat der Mensch Sprache.
nodes.trans: Already as an animal, man has language.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, U. of Chicago Press

nodes.author: lichtenberg
nodes.context: From Lichtenberg's Sudelbücher[waste books, notebooks].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: What a reader finds in a text depends on the reader.
nodes.orig: Ein Buch ist ein Spiegel, wenn ein Affe hineinguckt, so kann freilich kein Apostel heraus sehen.
nodes.trans: A book is a mirror: if an ape looks into it, an apostle can hardly look out.
nodes.sourceLabel: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, Sudelbücher, Heft E 215 (Promies numbering); cf. Aphorismen, ed. A. Leitzmann, 5 vols., Berlin 1902–08

nodes.author: kant
nodes.context: Said of Plato's word *Idee*[idea; eternal form].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The founding sentence of modern hermeneutics[theory of interpretation].
nodes.orig: …durch die Vergleichung der Gedanken, welche ein Verfasser über seinen Gegenstand äußert, ihn sogar besser zu verstehen, als er sich selbst verstand.
nodes.trans: …by comparing the thoughts an author expresses about his subject, to understand him even better than he understood himself.
nodes.sourceLabel: English, Meiklejohn, Gutenberg

nodes.author: lichtenberg
nodes.context: Another note from the Sudelbücher[waste books, notebooks].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Wittgenstein admired Lichtenberg; this could be the motto of the *Investigations*.
nodes.orig: Unsere ganze Philosophie ist Berichtigung des Sprachgebrauchs.
nodes.trans: Our whole philosophy is the correction of linguistic usage.
nodes.sourceLabel: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, Sudelbücher, Heft H 146 (Promies numbering); cf. Aphorismen, ed. A. Leitzmann, Berlin 1902–08

nodes.author: kant
nodes.context: Kant, in his lectures on anthropology, discusses thinking.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Thought is inner speech.
nodes.orig: Denken ist Reden mit sich selbst (die Indianer auf Otaheite nennen das Denken: die Sprache im Bauch).
nodes.trans: Thinking is speaking with oneself (the islanders of Tahiti call thinking 'speech in the belly').
nodes.sourceLabel: Immanuel Kant, Anthropologie in pragmatischer Hinsicht (1798), Erster Theil, Buch I, §39, Akademie-Ausgabe VII, p. 192, lines 31–34 (korpora.org)

nodes.author: talleyrand
nodes.context: A cynical saying of the diplomat Talleyrand. The attribution is traditional and unverified; the line has also been credited to Voltaire and to Fouché.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Speech as concealment, not expression.
nodes.orig: La parole a été donnée à l'homme pour déguiser sa pensée.
nodes.trans: Speech was given to man to disguise his thoughts.
nodes.sourceLabel: Attributed to Talleyrand by Bertrand Barère, Mémoires (1842); Fournier, L'Esprit dans l'histoire, says Harel put it in Talleyrand's mouth in Le Nain jaune (c. 1814–15). Earlier source: Voltaire, Dialogue du chapon et de la poularde (1763).

nodes.author: goethe
nodes.context: One of Goethe's maxims on art and culture.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: One's own language becomes visible only by comparison.
nodes.orig: Wer fremde Sprachen nicht kennt, weiß nichts von seiner eigenen.
nodes.trans: Whoever knows no foreign languages knows nothing of his own.
nodes.sourceLabel: J. W. von Goethe, Maximen und Reflexionen, ed. Max Hecker, Weimar: Goethe-Gesellschaft, 1907, no. 91 (first published in Über Kunst und Altertum III,1, 1821)

nodes.author: coleridge
nodes.context: Coleridge, talking at Highgate, distinguishes prose from poetry; his nephew records it in Table Talk.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Poetry differs from prose not in its ideas but in the choice of words themselves.
nodes.orig: …prose = words in their best order; poetry = the best words in the best order.
nodes.sourceLabel: Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Specimens of the Table Talk, 12 July 1827; Project Gutenberg #8489

nodes.author: humboldt
nodes.work: Über die Verschiedenheit des menschlichen Sprachbaues
nodes.context: Humboldt, introducing his study of the Kawi[Old Javanese] language, on the nature of language.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Chomsky built generative grammar on the second line.
nodes.orig: Die Sprache ist das bildende Organ des Gedanken.
nodes.trans: Language is the formative organ of thought…
nodes.sourceLabel: Wilhelm von Humboldt, Über die Kawi-Sprache auf der Insel Java, nebst einer Einleitung über die Verschiedenheit des menschlichen Sprachbaues…, Berlin: Königliche Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1836 (Internet Archive scan)

nodes.author: hugo
nodes.context: In 1482, the archdeacon Frollo stretches one hand toward a printed book on his table and the other toward the cathedral of Notre-Dame.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Medieval architecture was humanity's great book, written in stone for those who could not read; printing makes it obsolete. A new medium does not just carry the old content, it replaces the old medium. It is McLuhan's thesis in four words, 130 years early.
nodes.orig: Ceci tuera cela. Le livre tuera l'édifice.
nodes.trans: This will kill that. The book will kill the building.
nodes.sourceLabel: Victor Hugo, Notre-Dame de Paris (1831/1832), Livre V, ch. 2 « Ceci tuera cela »; Project Gutenberg #19657

nodes.author: kierkegaard
nodes.context: Johannes de silentio[Kierkegaard's pseudonym] praises Abraham. In substance: the poet cannot do what the hero does; he can only admire, love and rejoice in the hero, and his work is to keep the hero from being forgotten.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words cannot act; they can only remember. I have not confirmed the exact Danish wording, so it is paraphrased here.
nodes.sourceLabel: Frygt og Bæven, Danish, Det Kgl. Bibliotek

nodes.author: kierkegaard
nodes.context: Johannes de silentio[Kierkegaard's pseudonym] reflects on the poet, who can voice everything except his own hidden secret.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The poet's power over words is bought with one silence he can never break; speech is a devil's bargain.
nodes.orig: …kjøber denne Ordets Magt til at udsige alle Andres tunge Hemmeligheder for en lille Hemmelighed, han ikke kan udsige, og en Digter er ikke en Apostel, han uddriver kun Djævle ved Djævelens Magt.
nodes.trans: buys this power of the word, to utter everyone else's heavy secrets, at the price of one little secret he cannot utter; and a poet is not an apostle: he drives out devils only by the power of the devil.
nodes.sourceLabel: Frygt og Bæven, Danish, Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter

nodes.author: emerson
nodes.context: Emerson argues that every word began as a poet's image before use wore it down.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Language is fossil poetry: dead metaphors preserved like the archives of history.
nodes.orig: The poets made all the words, and therefore language is the archives of history, and, if we must say it, a sort of tomb of the muses… Language is fossil poetry.
nodes.sourceLabel: Ralph Waldo Emerson, 'The Poet', Essays: Second Series (1844); Project Gutenberg #2945

nodes.author: flaubert
nodes.context: The narrator comments as Emma pours out clichéd declarations to Rodolphe, who no longer hears the feeling behind them.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Speech is a cracked instrument: we aim at the stars and set bears dancing.
nodes.orig: …la parole humaine est comme un chaudron fêlé où nous battons des mélodies à faire danser les ours, quand on voudrait attendrir les étoiles.
nodes.trans: Human speech is like a cracked kettle on which we beat out tunes for bears to dance to, when we long to move the stars to pity.
nodes.sourceLabel: Gustave Flaubert, Madame Bovary (1857), Deuxième partie, ch. XII; Wikisource

nodes.author: carroll
nodes.context: At the Mad Tea-Party the March Hare and the Hatter catch Alice confusing saying with meaning.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Meaning what you say and saying what you mean are not the same thing.
nodes.orig: "Then you should say what you mean," the March Hare went on. "I do," Alice hastily replied; "at least—at least I mean what I say—that's the same thing, you know." "Not the same thing a bit!" said the Hatter.
nodes.sourceLabel: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Gutenberg

nodes.author: carroll
nodes.context: Alice finds a looking-glass book and reads "Jabberwocky". Alice: "Somehow it seems to fill my head with ideas—only I don't exactly know what they are!"
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A poem in which the grammar is perfectly clear and almost none of the words have meanings.
nodes.orig: 'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves / Did gyre and gimble in the wabe: / All mimsy were the borogoves, / And the mome raths outgrabe.
nodes.sourceLabel: Through the Looking-Glass, Gutenberg

nodes.author: carroll
nodes.context: Humpty Dumpty lectures Alice on words. He then glosses "Jabberwocky": "slithy" means "lithe and slimy… it's like a portmanteau[two-part travelling bag]—there are two meanings packed up into one word."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Meaning as power, a century before Foucault.
nodes.orig: "When I use a word," Humpty Dumpty said, in rather a scornful tone, "it means just what I choose it to mean—neither more nor less." "The question is," said Alice, "whether you can make words mean so many different things." "The question is," said Humpty Dumpty, "which is to be master—that's all."
nodes.sourceLabel: Through the Looking-Glass, Gutenberg

nodes.author: nietzsche
nodes.work: Über Wahrheit und Lüge im außermoralischen Sinne
nodes.context: In an unpublished early essay, Nietzsche asks where truth comes from.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Truths are worn-out metaphors whose origins we have forgotten; language manufactures truth.
nodes.orig: Was ist also Wahrheit? Ein bewegliches Heer von Metaphern, Metonymien, Anthropomorphismen… die Wahrheiten sind Illusionen, von denen man vergessen hat, dass sie welche sind.
nodes.trans: What then is truth? A mobile army of metaphors, metonymies, anthropomorphisms… truths are illusions we have forgotten are illusions.
nodes.sourceLabel: Friedrich Nietzsche, Ueber Wahrheit und Lüge im aussermoralischen Sinne (1873, Nachlass), §1; Digitale Kritische Gesamtausgabe (eKGWB WL-1), Nietzsche Source

nodes.author: mallarme
nodes.context: Mallarmé's memorial sonnet for Poe says the poet's task was to purify common language.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: T. S. Eliot echoes the line in "Little Gidding."
nodes.orig: Donner un sens plus pur aux mots de la tribu
nodes.trans: To give a purer sense to the words of the tribe.
nodes.sourceLabel: Stéphane Mallarmé, « Le Tombeau d'Edgar Poe » (1876/1877), l. 6; Wikisource

nodes.author: mallarme
nodes.context: Degas, struggling to write sonnets, complains that he is full of ideas; Mallarmé answers him.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Poems are made of words, not ideas.
nodes.orig: Ce n'est point avec des idées, mon cher Degas, que l'on fait des vers. C'est avec des mots.
nodes.trans: It is not with ideas, my dear Degas, that one makes verse. It is with words.
nodes.sourceLabel: Paul Valéry, Degas Danse Dessin (Paris: Ambroise Vollard, 1936; Gallimard, 1938)

nodes.author: nietzsche
nodes.context: Zarathustra, speaking in aphorisms himself, says what kind of writing he values.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The aphorist's answer to Plato: write so compactly that the text goes back into memory. An aphorism is writing designed to escape the page, which makes this the right entry for a collection of aphorisms.
nodes.orig: Von allem Geschriebenen liebe ich nur Das, was Einer mit seinem Blute schreibt.
nodes.trans: Of all that is written, I love only what a person writes with his blood.
nodes.sourceLabel: Friedrich Nietzsche, Also sprach Zarathustra I (1883), « Vom Lesen und Schreiben »; Project Gutenberg #7205

nodes.author: nietzsche
nodes.context: Zarathustra preaches to the crowd in the market square about the last man.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Creation, including creation in words, needs inner disorder.
nodes.orig: Ich sage euch: man muss noch Chaos in sich haben, um einen tanzenden Stern gebären zu können.
nodes.trans: I tell you: one must still have chaos in oneself to give birth to a dancing star.
nodes.sourceLabel: Also sprach Zarathustra, English, Gutenberg

nodes.author: nietzsche
nodes.context: Zarathustra's animals talk to him as he recovers from his collapse.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Speech does not capture things; it is a joyful folly that lets us dance over them.
nodes.orig: Sind nicht den Dingen Namen und Töne geschenkt, dass der Mensch sich an den Dingen erquicke? Es ist eine schöne Narrethei, das Sprechen: damit tanzt der Mensch über alle Dinge.
nodes.trans: Have not names and sounds been given to things so that man may refresh himself with things? Speaking is a beautiful folly: with it man dances over all things.
nodes.sourceLabel: Also sprach Zarathustra, English, Gutenberg

nodes.author: nietzsche
nodes.context: Nietzsche attacks the 'reason' of philosophers, which he traces to the subject–predicate structure of language.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A belated reply to John 1:1.
nodes.orig: Ich fürchte, wir werden Gott nicht los, weil wir noch an die Grammatik glauben…
nodes.trans: I fear we are not rid of God because we still have faith in grammar.
nodes.sourceLabel: Friedrich Nietzsche, Götzen-Dämmerung (1889), 'Die „Vernunft“ in der Philosophie' §5; eKGWB GD-Vernunft-5

nodes.author: mallarme
nodes.context: Mallarmé describes what happens when a poet names something.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The word summons the flower by abolishing every real one.
nodes.orig: Je dis: une fleur! et, hors de l'oubli où ma voix relègue aucun contour… musicalement se lève, idée même et suave, l'absente de tous bouquets.
nodes.trans: I say: a flower! and, out of the forgetting where my voice banishes every contour… there rises, musically, the very idea, delicate, the one absent from every bouquet.
nodes.sourceLabel: Stéphane Mallarmé, « Crise de vers », Divagations (Fasquelle, 1897); Wikisource

nodes.author: hofmannsthal
nodes.context: The fictional Lord Chandos explains to Francis Bacon why he has stopped writing.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Abstract language can fail all at once, decaying in the mouth.
nodes.orig: …die abstrakten Worte, deren sich doch die Zunge naturgemäß bedienen muß, um irgendwelches Urteil an den Tag zu geben, zerfielen mir im Munde wie modrige Pilze.
nodes.trans: The abstract words which the tongue must naturally use to bring any judgment to light crumbled in my mouth like mouldy mushrooms.
nodes.sourceLabel: Hugo von Hofmannsthal, « Ein Brief », Der Tag (Berlin), 18–19 Oct. 1902; repr. Die prosaischen Schriften gesammelt, 1907

nodes.author: saussure
nodes.context: Saussure's Geneva lectures, reconstructed by his students, define the linguistic sign.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Meaning is not attached to things but arises from differences within the system of language.
nodes.orig:
Le lien unissant le signifiant au signifié est arbitraire.
…dans la langue il n'y a que des différences sans termes positifs.
nodes.trans: The bond between the signifier and the signified is arbitrary… in language there are only differences, without positive terms.
nodes.sourceLabel: Ferdinand de Saussure, Cours de linguistique générale (1916), Ire partie ch. I §2 and IIe partie ch. IV §4; Wikisource

nodes.author: eliot
nodes.work: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
nodes.context: Prufrock, at an evening party, despairs of saying anything properly.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The gap between meaning and saying.
nodes.orig: It is impossible to say just what I mean!
nodes.sourceLabel: Prufrock and Other Observations, Gutenberg

nodes.author: wittgenstein
nodes.context: Wittgenstein's numbered propositions on logic, world and language. Ogden's 1922 version of 7: "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Language pictures the world up to a limit; beyond it lies what can only be shown, and the book itself is a ladder to throw away.
nodes.orig:
1 — Die Welt ist alles, was der Fall ist.
4.0031 — Alle Philosophie ist »Sprachkritik«.
5.6 — Die Grenzen meiner Sprache bedeuten die Grenzen meiner Welt.
5.62 — …daß die Welt meine Welt ist…
6.522 — Es gibt allerdings Unaussprechliches. Dies zeigt sich, es ist das Mystische.
6.54 — Er muß sozusagen die Leiter wegwerfen, nachdem er auf ihr hinaufgestiegen ist.
7 — Wovon man nicht sprechen kann, darüber muß man schweigen.
nodes.trans: The world is all that is the case… All philosophy is 'critique of language'… The limits of my language mean the limits of my world… the world is my world… There is indeed the inexpressible. This shows itself; it is the mystical… He must, so to speak, throw away the ladder after he has climbed up it… What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence
nodes.sourceLabel: German–English, Ogden, Gutenberg

nodes.author: wittgenstein
nodes.context: Wittgenstein writes to the publisher Ludwig von Ficker about the Tractatus.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The unsaid part of the book is the important one.
nodes.orig: …mein Werk bestehe aus zwei Teilen: aus dem, der hier vorliegt, und aus alledem, was ich *nicht* geschrieben habe. Und gerade dieser zweite Teil ist der Wichtige.
nodes.trans: My work consists of two parts: the one presented here, and all that I have *not* written. And it is precisely this second part that is the important one.
nodes.sourceLabel: Wittgenstein, letter to Ludwig von Ficker, Oct./Nov. 1919; printed in Briefe an Ludwig von Ficker, ed. G. H. von Wright (Salzburg: Otto Müller, 1969)

nodes.author: einstein
nodes.context: Einstein lectures to the Prussian Academy of Sciences on how geometry relates to physical bodies.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: This is the gap between a formal language and the world.
nodes.orig: Insofern sich die Sätze der Mathematik auf die Wirklichkeit beziehen, sind sie nicht sicher, und insofern sie sicher sind, beziehen sie sich nicht auf die Wirklichkeit.
nodes.trans: As far as the laws of mathematics refer to reality, they are not certain; and as far as they are certain, they do not refer to reality.
nodes.sourceLabel: Albert Einstein, Geometrie und Erfahrung: Erweiterte Fassung des Festvortrages gehalten an der Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin am 27. Januar 1921 (Berlin: Springer, 1921), pp. 3–4

nodes.author: einstein
nodes.context: Said in conversation at Princeton during his first American visit, on hearing of an experiment that seemed to contradict relativity; later carved over a fireplace in Fine Hall.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: This one fits the "nature of gods" thread: the Lord is raffiniert[subtle, cunning], hidden but not deceitful, so nature can be read.
nodes.orig: Raffiniert ist der Herrgott, aber boshaft ist er nicht.
nodes.trans: Subtle is the Lord, but malicious He is not.
nodes.sourceLabel: Oral remark at Princeton, May 1921, reportedly to Oswald Veblen; later carved over the fireplace of the common room in old Fine Hall (now Jones Hall), Princeton. See Abraham Pais, 'Subtle is the Lord...': The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein (Oxford UP, 1982)

nodes.author: eliot
nodes.context: The poem ends in a collage of English, Italian, Latin, French and Sanskrit: "Give. Sympathize. Control. / Peace." Datta, Dayadhvam, Damyata are the thunder's words from the Upanishads[Hindu scriptures].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A Babel deliberately rebuilt from fragments.
nodes.orig: These fragments I have shored against my ruins… / Datta. Dayadhvam. Damyata. / Shantih shantih shantih
nodes.sourceLabel: The Waste Land, Gutenberg

nodes.author: eliot
nodes.context: The quotations nest four deep. Eliot quotes Petronius, whose drunken host Trimalchio quotes the boys and the Sibyl[ancient prophetess], and the boys and Sibyl speak Greek inside Trimalchio's Latin. The poem opens in two dead languages before it reaches English.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The Sibyl was granted a thousand years without youth and shrank until only her voice remained. In Ovid she says it herself (Metamorphoses 14.153): voce tamen noscar; vocem mihi fata relinquent, "yet by my voice I shall be known; the fates will leave me my voice." Language is what outlives the speaker.
nodes.orig: Nam Sibyllam quidem Cumis ego ipse oculis meis vidi in ampulla pendere, et cum illi pueri dicerent: Σίβυλλα τί θέλεις; respondebat illa: ἀποθανεῖν θέλω.
nodes.trans: For I myself saw with my own eyes the Sibyl at Cumae hanging in a jar, and when the boys asked her, 'Sibyl, what do you want?' she answered, 'I want to die.'" The quotations nest four deep. Eliot quotes Petronius, whose drunken host Trimalchio quotes the boys and the Sibyl, and the boys and Sibyl speak Greek inside Trimalchio's Latin. The poem opens in two dead languages before it reaches English. The Sibyl was granted a thousand years without youth and shrank until only her voice remained. In Ovid she says it herself (*Metamorphoses* 14.153): *voce tamen noscar; vocem mihi fata relinquent*, "yet by my voice I shall be known; the fates will leave me my voice.
nodes.sourceLabel: The Waste Land, Gutenberg

nodes.author: einstein
nodes.context: Writing to Max Born on quantum mechanics.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: He is convinced that God "does not throw dice": the laws of nature must be sentences without chance in their grammar.
nodes.orig: Jedenfalls bin ich überzeugt, daß der nicht würfelt.
nodes.trans: At any rate, I am convinced that He does not throw dice.
nodes.sourceLabel: Einstein to Max Born, 4 December 1926, in Albert Einstein – Hedwig und Max Born: Briefwechsel 1916–1955 (Munich: Nymphenburger, 1969); Eng. The Born–Einstein Letters (London: Macmillan, 1971); Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, vol. 15, doc. 426

nodes.author: heisenberg
nodes.work: Über den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik
nodes.context: Heisenberg says a word like "position" means nothing unless you can name the experiment that measures it.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The 1927 uncertainty paper is really an argument about meaning. Because position and momentum can't both be measured precisely, the words can't both apply precisely at once.
nodes.sourceLabel: Werner Heisenberg, 'Über den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik', Zeitschrift für Physik 43, no. 3–4 (1927): 172–198 (received 23 March 1927)

nodes.author: ramsey
nodes.context: Ramsey answers the Tractatus's ending.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: If something cannot be said, it cannot be hinted at either.
nodes.orig: But what we can't say we can't say, and we can't whistle it either.
nodes.sourceLabel: F. P. Ramsey, 'General Propositions and Causality' (1929), in The Foundations of Mathematics and Other Logical Essays, ed. R. B. Braithwaite (London: Kegan Paul, 1931), p. 238 (bracketed passage)

nodes.author: godel
nodes.work: Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica und verwandter Systeme I
nodes.context: Gödel assigns every symbol and formula a number, so arithmetic can talk about its own sentences. He then builds a sentence that, in effect, says "I am not provable"; in the paper he notes the analogy with the Liar and with Richard's paradox[self-referential definability paradox] himself.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: If the system is consistent, that sentence is true but can't be proved inside the system. It belongs in the same family as Quine's paradox, and echoes Tractatus 6.522, "this shows itself," and Revelation 2:17's name that only its holder knows. Any language rich enough to describe itself contains truths it can't reach.
nodes.sourceLabel: Kurt Gödel, 'Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica und verwandter Systeme I', Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik 38 (1931): 173–198

nodes.author: neurath
nodes.context: Neurath's 1932 paper on protocol sentences[basic observation reports]; Quine took this passage as the epigraph to Word and Object.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: No language can be rebuilt from outside itself; we revise it while using it.
nodes.orig: Wie Schiffer sind wir, die ihr Schiff auf offener See umbauen müssen, ohne es jemals in einem Dock zerlegen und aus besten Bestandteilen neu errichten zu können.
nodes.trans: We are like sailors who must rebuild their ship on the open sea, without ever being able to dismantle it in dock and reconstruct it from the best parts.
nodes.sourceLabel: Otto Neurath, 'Protokollsätze', Erkenntnis 3 (1932/33): 204-214

nodes.author: bloomfield
nodes.context: Leonard Bloomfield, a founding figure of American linguistics, on Pāṇini's Sanskrit grammar, which, he adds, describes every inflection, derivation, and syntactic usage of its author's speech.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A grammar that generates a whole language from a few thousand explicit rules, ranked among humanity's greatest achievements. Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī[Pāṇini's grammar] is the ancestor of generative grammar and of the notations, like BNF[Backus–Naur Form], that define programming languages.
nodes.orig: This grammar […] is one of the greatest monuments of human intelligence.
nodes.sourceLabel: Leonard Bloomfield, Language (New York: Henry Holt, 1933), ch. 1, p. 11

nodes.author: einstein
nodes.context: Einstein's essay on the method of physics, printed in German with an English translation.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: That the world can be put into concepts at all is the one thing that cannot itself be explained.
nodes.orig: Das ewig Unbegreifliche an der Welt ist ihre Begreiflichkeit.
nodes.trans: The eternally incomprehensible thing about the world is its comprehensibility.
nodes.sourceLabel: Albert Einstein, 'Physik und Realität', Journal of the Franklin Institute 221, no. 3 (March 1936): 313–347 (German text with English translation 'Physics and Reality' by Jean Piccard)

nodes.author: turing
nodes.work: On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem
nodes.context: Turing defines computation as a person reading and writing symbols on a tape, to settle Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem[decision problem].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Thought is modeled as writing.
nodes.sourceLabel: A. M. Turing, 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem', Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society s2-42 (1936–37): 230–265 (received 28 May 1936, read 12 November 1936)

nodes.author: eliot
nodes.context: In copyright, paraphrased. In "Burnt Norton" V, words strain and crack under their burden and will not stay still. In "East Coker" V, each new attempt at writing is a fresh raid on what cannot yet be said, with worn-out equipment. In "Little Gidding" II, a ghost recalls that the poet's task was to purify the dialect of the tribe, translating Mallarmé's line.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words never hold still; each poem is a new attempt with failing tools.
nodes.sourceLabel: T. S. Eliot, Four Quartets (New York: Harcourt, 1943; London: Faber & Faber, 1944)

nodes.author: cs-lewis
nodes.context: Lewis's essay on metaphor, later collected; his Studies in Words (1960) traces how words like "nature" and "world" shifted meaning.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: All our language about abstract things is buried metaphor, and we think truly with a metaphor only if we remember it is one.
nodes.sourceLabel: C. S. Lewis, 'Bluspels and Flalansferes: A Semantic Nightmare', in Rehabilitations and Other Essays (OUP, 1939); repr. Selected Literary Essays (CUP, 1969)

nodes.author: turing
nodes.work: Wittgenstein's Lectures on the Foundations of Mathematics, Cambridge 1939
nodes.context: Turing attends Wittgenstein's 1939 Cambridge lectures on the foundations of mathematics, and they argue there about whether a hidden contradiction in a calculus matters.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The machine's inventor and the philosopher of meaning-as-use dispute what a formal language's contradictions mean. Those notes are published as Wittgenstein's Lectures on the Foundations of Mathematics (ed. Diamond).
nodes.sourceLabel: Wittgenstein's Lectures on the Foundations of Mathematics, Cambridge, 1939, from the notes of R. G. Bosanquet, Norman Malcolm, Rush Rhees, and Yorick Smythies, ed. Cora Diamond (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1976)

nodes.author: tolkien
nodes.context: Tolkien's Andrew Lang Lecture on fantasy, arguing about where fairy-stories come from.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Tolkien argues that the adjective is a magic word: whoever can lift green from grass and set it on the sun already holds an enchanter's power, and fantasy is born in grammar. Mind, tongue and tale are coeval[of equal age].
nodes.orig: …the incarnate mind, the tongue, and the tale are in our world coeval.
nodes.sourceLabel: J. R. R. Tolkien, 'On Fairy-Stories' (Andrew Lang Lecture, St Andrews, 8 March 1939), in Tree and Leaf (Allen & Unwin, 1964)

nodes.author: wittgenstein
