nodes.context: Wittgenstein's later remarks, numbered sections and the former "Part II" (PPF = the former "Part II.").
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Meaning is use within a form of life; philosophy fights the spells language casts.
nodes.orig:
§19 — …eine Sprache vorstellen heißt, sich eine Lebensform vorstellen.
§43 — Die Bedeutung eines Wortes ist sein Gebrauch in der Sprache.
§109 — Die Philosophie ist ein Kampf gegen die Verhexung unseres Verstandes durch die Mittel unserer Sprache.
PPF §327 — Wenn ein Löwe sprechen könnte, wir könnten ihn nicht verstehen.
nodes.trans: To imagine a language means to imagine a form of life… The meaning of a word is its use in the language… Philosophy is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of our language… If a lion could talk, we could not understand him.
nodes.sourceLabel: Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations, rev. 4th ed., trans. G. E. M. Anscombe, P. M. S. Hacker and J. Schulte (Wiley-Blackwell, 2009), §§19, 43, 109; PPF §327

nodes.author: oppenheimer
nodes.context: Oppenheimer told Groves he thought the name "Trinity" came from John Donne's Holy Sonnet XIV (published 1633), whose first line he quoted.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The first nuclear explosion was named from a poem.
nodes.orig: Batter my heart, three-person'd God…
nodes.sourceLabel: J. Robert Oppenheimer, letter to Gen. Leslie R. Groves, 20 Oct. 1962, replying to Groves's question about the name 'Trinity'; quoted in R. Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)

nodes.author: cs-lewis
nodes.context: At the novel's Babel, the conspirators' banquet dissolves into gibberish.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Lewis's own Latin: those who despise the divine Word lose human speech too.
nodes.orig: Qui Verbum Dei contempserunt, eis auferetur etiam verbum hominis.
nodes.trans: They that have despised the Word of God, from them shall the word of man also be taken away.
nodes.sourceLabel: C. S. Lewis, That Hideous Strength (London: John Lane The Bodley Head, 1945)

nodes.author: einstein
nodes.context: Answering Hadamard's survey of how mathematicians think, he says written or spoken words play no part; he thought in images and "muscular" signs and searched for words only afterward.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: This is the strongest counterexample in the collection to "thinking is speaking with oneself."
nodes.orig: do not seem to play any role in my mechanism of thought
nodes.sourceLabel: Einstein to Jacques Hadamard (c. 1945), printed in Hadamard, An Essay on the Psychology of Invention in the Mathematical Field (Princeton UP, 1945; Dover repr. 1954), Appendix II

nodes.placeName: Trinity site, Jornada del Muerto, New Mexico
nodes.author: oppenheimer
nodes.work: The Decision to Drop the Bomb
nodes.context: Watching the Trinity explosion, as recalled in 1965. Oppenheimer studied Sanskrit at Berkeley with Arthur W. Ryder from 1933 and read the Gita in the original. The line is his own rendering of Gita 11.32 (kālo 'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt[Time, world-destroyer]), where kāla[time; death] is literally "Time."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Earlier printed versions of the anecdote (William Laurence, Robert Jungk) have "the shatterer of worlds." The most famous sentence of the atomic age is a translation, and it exists in competing versions. On the sources: James Hijiya, "The Gita of J. Robert Oppenheimer" (2000).
nodes.orig: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.
nodes.sourceLabel: J. Robert Oppenheimer, interview in 'The Decision to Drop the Bomb' (NBC White Paper, 1965), recalling the Trinity test of 16 July 1945

nodes.author: orwell
nodes.context: Orwell's essay on the decay of political English. Political language, he adds, is built to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Thucydides 3.82, restated.
nodes.orig: But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.
nodes.sourceLabel: George Orwell, 'Politics and the English Language', Horizon 13, no. 76 (April 1946)

nodes.author: heidegger
nodes.context: Heidegger replies to Jean Beaufret about humanism. Heidegger draws on Hölderlin's late line, "…dichterisch wohnet / Der Mensch auf dieser Erde" ("poetically / man dwells on this earth").
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Language is not a tool we use but the dwelling in which we exist.
nodes.orig: Die Sprache ist das Haus des Seins. In ihrer Behausung wohnt der Mensch.
nodes.trans: Language is the house of Being. In its home human beings dwell.
nodes.sourceLabel: Heidegger, 'Brief über den »Humanismus«', in Wegmarken, GA 9 (Frankfurt: Klostermann), opening paragraph; English 'Letter on Humanism' in Basic Writings, ed. D. F. Krell (Harper)

nodes.author: oppenheimer
nodes.context: Oppenheimer's Arthur D. Little Memorial Lecture at MIT, two years after Hiroshima.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Genesis 3 in the language of physics.
nodes.orig: …the physicists have known sin; and this is a knowledge which they cannot lose.
nodes.sourceLabel: J. Robert Oppenheimer, "Physics in the Contemporary World" (Arthur D. Little Memorial Lecture, MIT, 25 Nov 1947), Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists 4:3 (March 1948), pp. 65-68

nodes.author: orwell
nodes.context: Syme, the lexicographer, explains that the dictionary is shrinking every year.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The appendix, "The Principles of Newspeak," describes a language built to make heresy literally unsayable. (Orwell died in 1950, so his works are public domain in Canada.)
nodes.orig: Don't you see that the whole aim of Newspeak is to narrow the range of thought?
nodes.sourceLabel: George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four (Secker & Warburg, 1949), Part I ch. 5 (Syme)

nodes.author: quine
nodes.context: Quine's essay on ontological commitment[assumed existents]. The same book holds "Two Dogmas of Empiricism" (1951), where statements face experience only "as a corporate body."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Meaning is what essence becomes when it moves from things to words.
nodes.orig: To be is to be the value of a variable.
nodes.sourceLabel: W. V. Quine, 'On What There Is', Review of Metaphysics 2, no. 5 (Sept. 1948): 21-38; repr. From a Logical Point of View (Harvard UP, 1953)

nodes.author: turing
nodes.context: Turing opens by posing the question, then immediately sets it aside because the meanings of "machine" and "think" can't be settled, and replaces it with the imitation game, a test carried out entirely in typed language. He predicts that by the century's end people will speak of machines thinking without being contradicted.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: That makes him Descartes' heir and the Voigt-Kampff[Blade Runner empathy-test] test's ancestor. Like Horace's usus[usage], or Wittgenstein's meaning-as-use, usage decides.
nodes.orig: I propose to consider the question, "Can machines think?"
nodes.sourceLabel: A. M. Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind 59, no. 236 (October 1950): 433–460, §1 'The Imitation Game' and §6

nodes.author: innis
nodes.context: An economic historian of the fur trade and the cod fisheries turns to the materials of writing. Durable, heavy media such as stone and clay favor empires that last in time; light ones such as papyrus and paper favor empires that spread across space.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The physical weight of a medium shapes what a civilization can remember and how far it can reach. McLuhan called his own Gutenberg Galaxy a footnote to Innis.
nodes.sourceLabel: Harold A. Innis, The Bias of Communication (University of Toronto Press, 1951)

nodes.author: oppenheimer
nodes.context: Oppenheimer asks whether an electron's position stays the same, changes with time, stands still, or moves, and answers each question "no."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Ordinary language, built for a world of tables and stones, gives wrong answers at the scale of the atom. Physics must speak, as Bohr held, in complementary descriptions that cannot be combined into one picture.
nodes.sourceLabel: J. Robert Oppenheimer, Science and the Common Understanding (Simon & Schuster / Oxford UP, 1954) [BBC Reith Lectures 1953]

nodes.author: tolkien
nodes.context: The inscription on the Doors of Durin. Gandalf fails to open them until he reads the sentence literally: the password is the Elvish word for "friend," mellon[Elvish: friend].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The puzzle is a lesson in ambiguity.
nodes.orig: Speak, friend, and enter.
nodes.sourceLabel: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring (Allen & Unwin, 1954), Book II ch. 4 'A Journey in the Dark'

nodes.author: levi-strauss
nodes.context: Among the Nambikwara of Mato Grosso, who have no writing, a chief imitates the anthropologist's note-taking by scribbling wavy lines, then "reads" them aloud to his people to show his power over them.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The darkest theory of writing here: it arose to let states count, tax, and conscript people, not to spread knowledge. The chief grasps what writing is for before he grasps what it says. Derrida's Of Grammatology contests this chapter at length.
nodes.orig: …la fonction primaire de la communication écrite est de faciliter l'asservissement.
nodes.trans: …the primary function of written communication is to facilitate enslavement.
nodes.sourceLabel: Claude Lévi-Strauss, Tristes Tropiques (Paris: Plon, 1955), ch. XXVIII "Leçon d'écriture"; English trans. John Russell (Criterion, 1961)

nodes.author: cs-lewis
nodes.context: Aslan sings Narnia into being, and stars, grass, and animals appear as the song changes.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Uncle Andrew hears only roaring, because he has decided not to hear words.
nodes.sourceLabel: C. S. Lewis, The Magician's Nephew (London: The Bodley Head, 1955)

nodes.author: tolkien
nodes.work: The Letters of J. R. R. Tolkien
nodes.context: Writing to his American publisher, Tolkien explains how The Lord of the Rings began. He continues that the stories were made to give the languages a world, not the other way round.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Middle-earth exists so that Elvish could have speakers.
nodes.orig: The invention of languages is the foundation.
nodes.sourceLabel: The Letters of J. R. R. Tolkien, ed. H. Carpenter with C. Tolkien, letter 165 (to Houghton Mifflin, June 1955)

nodes.author: cs-lewis
nodes.context: Orual realizes that saying exactly what you mean, the whole of it and nothing else, is "the whole art and joy of words."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The complaint she spent her life composing was itself the answer.
nodes.orig: How can they meet us face to face till we have faces?
nodes.sourceLabel: C. S. Lewis, Till We Have Faces (London: Geoffrey Bles, 1956), Part I, final chapter

nodes.author: chomsky
nodes.work: Three Models for the Description of Language
nodes.ref: IRE Transactions on Information Theory IT-2.3
nodes.context: The paper that defines the hierarchy of grammars, from finite-state[fixed finite memory] to unrestricted, by the power of the rules each allows. It argues that English cannot be generated by a finite-state machine.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A model of human speech becomes the classification every parser is still built on.
nodes.sourceLabel: Noam Chomsky, 'Three Models for the Description of Language', IRE Transactions on Information Theory IT-2, no. 3 (September 1956): 113–124

nodes.author: chomsky
nodes.context: A sentence that is perfectly grammatical and means nothing, set beside its reversal, Furiously sleep ideas green colorless, which is neither.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Grammaticality is not meaning. Chomsky defines the grammar of a language as a device that generates all of its grammatical sequences and none of the ungrammatical ones.
nodes.orig: Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.
nodes.sourceLabel: Noam Chomsky, Syntactic Structures (The Hague: Mouton, 1957; 2nd ed. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2002), ch. 2 'The Independence of Grammar', p. 15, example (1)

nodes.author: heisenberg
nodes.context: From his Gifford Lectures on the Copenhagen interpretation, first published in English.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The answer depends on the grammar of the question.
nodes.orig: What we observe is not nature in itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.
nodes.sourceLabel: Werner Heisenberg, Physics and Philosophy: The Revolution in Modern Science (New York: Harper & Row, 1958), ch. III 'The Copenhagen Interpretation of Quantum Theory'

nodes.author: backus
nodes.work: The Syntax and Semantics of the Proposed International Algebraic Language
nodes.context: Backus defines the syntax of what became ALGOL with a new notation of "metalinguistic formulae": a named class is defined as a choice among sequences of symbols and other named classes.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: He later said he had adapted Emil Post's production systems; he had not yet read Chomsky.
nodes.sourceLabel: J. W. Backus, 'The Syntax and Semantics of the Proposed International Algebraic Language of the Zurich ACM-GAMM Conference', Proceedings of the International Conference on Information Processing, UNESCO, Paris, June 1959 (publ. 1960), pp. 125–132

nodes.author: quine
nodes.context: The opening sentence. Chapter 2 introduces "Gavagai": a linguist watches a speaker point at a rabbit and cannot settle, even in principle, whether the word means rabbit, rabbit-stage, or undetached rabbit parts.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: This is the indeterminacy of translation. Quine's slogan elsewhere: "No entity without identity."
nodes.orig: Language is a social art.
nodes.sourceLabel: W. V. Quine, Word and Object (MIT Press, 1960; new ed. 2013), Preface, p. ix

nodes.author: lord
nodes.context: Lord completes Milman Parry's study of illiterate South Slavic bards, recorded in the 1930s. A guslar[Balkan epic singer] doesn't recite a memorized text; he recomposes the song in each performance, from inherited formulas and themes.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: This is how Homer's "winged words" and "rosy-fingered Dawn" work: they are metrical building blocks for composing aloud. In an oral tradition there is no fixed text, so writing created the very idea of "the original."
nodes.orig: In a sense each performance is "an" original, if not "the" original.
nodes.sourceLabel: Albert B. Lord, The Singer of Tales (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1960; 2nd ed., ed. S. Mitchell and G. Nagy, 2000), ch. 5 'Songs and the Song'; online edition at the Center for Hellenic Studies

nodes.author: mcluhan
nodes.context: McLuhan argues that the printed book made Western man linear, private, and visual, and that electric media are now undoing it.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Print left each reader alone with a page; electric media return humanity to something like tribal, oral simultaneity. The phrase "global village" starts here, three decades before the web. The phonetic alphabet, he argues, gave its users "an eye for an ear," moving knowledge from hearing to seeing.
nodes.orig: The new electronic interdependence recreates the world in the image of a global village.
nodes.sourceLabel: Marshall McLuhan, The Gutenberg Galaxy: The Making of Typographic Man (University of Toronto Press, 1962)

nodes.author: tolkien
nodes.context: The world begins as music: Ilúvatar gives the Ainur[angelic powers] themes, they sing, and the song becomes the world.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: It is Genesis 1 rewritten as polyphony[many-voiced music], including a discord. Tolkien's 1936 lecture "Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics" is still the best-known essay on the poem.
nodes.sourceLabel: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Silmarillion, ed. C. Tolkien (Allen & Unwin, 1977), 'Ainulindalë'

nodes.author: havelock
nodes.context: Havelock asks why Plato's Republic banishes the poets, and answers that Homeric poetry was Greece's encyclopedia: a society's knowledge stored in memorized verse.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Plato's attack on poetry is literacy's attack on oral memory, the mind's shift from reciting to analyzing. Read this way, the Phaedrus is the old order's last protest, written in the new order's medium.
nodes.sourceLabel: Eric A. Havelock, Preface to Plato (Harvard University Press, 1963)

nodes.author: naur
nodes.work: Revised Report on the Algorithmic Language ALGOL 60
nodes.context: Naur simplified Backus's notation and edited the report with it, and the notation became Backus–Naur Form. Its rules read like `<digit> ::= 0 | 1 | 2 …`, where `::=` is pronounced "is defined as" and `|` is "or."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Nearly every programming language since has been specified this way.
nodes.orig: The syntax will be described with the aid of metalinguistic formulae.
nodes.sourceLabel: Revised Report, masswerk.at

nodes.author: philip-k-dick
nodes.context: The Man in the High Castle (1962): characters steer their lives by the I Ching[Chinese oracle book], an oracle that, like Heraclitus's at Delphi, gives signs. Martian Time-Slip (1964): a boy's collapsing sense of time turns speech into "gubble."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Gubble is language as entropy. Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968): humanity is tested by a conversation, the Voigt-Kampff interview, an heir of Descartes' language test. A Scanner Darkly (1977): titled from 1 Corinthians 13:12.
nodes.sourceLabel: Philip K. Dick, novels 1961-1977 (various publishers)

nodes.author: mcluhan
nodes.work: Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man
nodes.context: The book's first chapter, "The Medium Is the Message," argues that every medium is an extension of the body or senses, and that its effects come from its form, not from what it carries.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Content is a distraction. Electric light carries no message, yet it remakes how people live; what matters is the change of scale, pace, or pattern a medium introduces. Each medium wraps the one before it, as every render target wraps the languages beneath it.
nodes.orig: The medium is the message.
nodes.sourceLabel: Marshall McLuhan, Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man (McGraw-Hill, 1964), ch. 1 "The Medium Is the Message"

nodes.author: chomsky
nodes.work: Aspects of the Theory of Syntax
nodes.context: Chomsky separates competence[speaker's tacit knowledge], a speaker's knowledge of the language, from performance[actual speech use], its use in actual speech, with its slips and limits. The grammar models competence.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Here he takes up Humboldt's "infinite use of finite means" (see above) as the problem a grammar must solve.
nodes.sourceLabel: Noam Chomsky, Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1965), ch. 1 'Methodological Preliminaries'

nodes.author: foucault
nodes.context: The book was born, Foucault says, from laughing at a passage in Borges that cites a "certain Chinese encyclopedia" dividing animals into those belonging to the Emperor, embalmed ones, those drawn with a very fine camelhair brush, and so on.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The laughter exposes the limits of our own categories: what is impossible is not the animals but the space of language where they could sit side by side.
nodes.sourceLabel: Michel Foucault, Les Mots et les choses (Paris: Gallimard, 1966), Préface; English: The Order of Things (Pantheon, 1970)

nodes.author: foucault
nodes.context: The closing pages of The Order of Things. He ends by suggesting that man may be erased like a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: "Man" is a recent arrangement of words, not a permanent fact.
nodes.orig: L'homme est une invention dont l'archéologie de notre pensée montre aisément la date récente.
nodes.trans: Man is an invention of recent date, as the archaeology of our thought easily shows.
nodes.sourceLabel: Michel Foucault, Les Mots et les choses (Gallimard, 1966), ch. X "Les sciences humaines", sect. VI (usually cited p. 398); English: The Order of Things (1970), p. 387

nodes.author: derrida
nodes.context: The book's long middle section reads Rousseau's Essai sur l'origine des langues.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Often mistranslated as "there is nothing outside the text"; the claim is that there is no reading that escapes interpretation, not that the world is made of words.
nodes.orig: Il n'y a pas de hors-texte.
nodes.trans: There is no outside-text.
nodes.sourceLabel: Jacques Derrida, De la grammatologie (Paris: Minuit, 1967), Part II ch. 2 "...Ce dangereux supplément...", p. 227 (Spivak trans., Johns Hopkins UP 1976, p. 158)

nodes.author: mcluhan
nodes.work: The Medium Is the Massage (with Quentin Fiore)
nodes.context: A collage of text and images designed by Quentin Fiore. The title's "Massage" was a typesetter's error, which McLuhan is said to have kept with delight.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A misprint that proves the thesis: the medium massages its users, and the title also reads "Mess Age" and "Mass Age." It is the only entry here whose most famous word is a typo.
nodes.sourceLabel: Marshall McLuhan & Quentin Fiore, The Medium Is the Massage: An Inventory of Effects (Bantam, 1967; Gingko Press, 2001)

nodes.author: ingerman
nodes.context: Writing as manager of language systems at RCA, Ingerman answers Knuth's 1964 letter on the name "Backus Normal Form": Pāṇini had used an equivalent notation for Sanskrit, so the form should be renamed.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The rename didn't stick, but "Backus–Naur Form" (see below) did.
nodes.orig: Since it is traditional in professional circles to give credit where credit is due, and since there is clear evidence that Panini was the earlier independent inventor of the notation, may I suggest the name "Panini-Backus Form" as being a more desirable one? Not only does it give due credit, but it also avoids the misuse of the word "Normal."
nodes.sourceLabel: Peter Zilahy Ingerman, letter to the editor, Communications of the ACM 10(3), March 1967, p. 137; ACM Digital Library

nodes.author: culkin
nodes.context: Culkin, a Jesuit at Fordham, summarizes McLuhan for teachers.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Usually credited to McLuhan, but it is Culkin's summary of him; it anticipates Dijkstra on tools and thinking habits by eight years. The misattribution is itself a small media effect: the famous name absorbs the line.
nodes.orig: We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us.
nodes.sourceLabel: John M. Culkin, "A Schoolman's Guide to Marshall McLuhan," Saturday Review, 18 March 1967, start p. 51 (quote pp. 53 and 70)

nodes.author: star-trek
nodes.context: Kirk's crew uses the universal translator to speak with a non-corporeal being, the Companion.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The device rests on the assumption that all minds share an underlying grammar, close to Humboldt and Chomsky.
nodes.sourceLabel: Star Trek, 'Metamorphosis', TOS season 2 episode 9 (prod. 31), NBC, 1967-11-10

nodes.author: derrida
nodes.context: A reading of the Phaedrus passage above, built on the double sense of pharmakon[remedy and poison].
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Writing, Derrida argues, was always already inside the speech that claimed to be its master.
nodes.sourceLabel: Jacques Derrida, "La pharmacie de Platon" (Tel Quel 32-33, 1968), repr. in La Dissémination (Paris: Seuil, 1972); English: Dissemination, trans. Barbara Johnson (U. of Chicago Press, 1981)

nodes.author: philip-k-dick
nodes.context: Each chapter opens with an advertising jingle for the product Ubik. In the final epigraph, Ubik speaks in the cadence of John 1: it was before the universe, it made the suns and worlds, and it calls itself the word, whose name is never spoken and which no one knows.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: John's prologue and Revelation's secret name (2:17), voiced by a spray can.
nodes.sourceLabel: Philip K. Dick, Ubik (Doubleday, 1969)

nodes.author: derrida
nodes.context: Derrida coins différance[differing and deferring], with an a, to name meaning as both differing (Saussure) and deferring.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The misspelling cannot be heard in French; it exists only in writing, which is the point.
nodes.sourceLabel: Jacques Derrida, "La différance" (lecture, Société française de philosophie, 27 Jan 1968), in Marges de la philosophie (Paris: Minuit, 1972)

nodes.author: dijkstra
nodes.context: So the programmer should make the correspondence between the program, "spread out in text space," and the process, "spread out in time," as trivial as possible. Dijkstra's title was "A Case against the GO TO Statement"; the famous one was supplied by the editor, Niklaus Wirth.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: A text should show the shape of what it does.
nodes.orig: …our intellectual powers are rather geared to master static relations and… our powers to visualize processes evolving in time are relatively poorly developed.
nodes.sourceLabel: EWD 215, UT Austin

nodes.author: heisenberg
nodes.context: Heisenberg records Niels Bohr telling him this on a walk in 1922; the words are Bohr's, as Heisenberg reconstructed them decades later.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Where pictures fail, words cannot describe; like Dichtung[poetry], they can only evoke.
nodes.orig: Wenn es um Atome geht, kann die Sprache nur so verwendet werden wie in der Dichtung.
nodes.trans: When it comes to atoms, language can be used only as in poetry.
nodes.sourceLabel: Werner Heisenberg, Der Teil und das Ganze: Gespräche im Umkreis der Atomphysik, Piper, München, 1969, Kap. 3 'Der Begriff "Verstehen" in der modernen Physik (1920–1922)' (words attributed to Niels Bohr)

speaker.name: Niels Bohr
speaker.note: as reported by Heisenberg in Der Teil und das Ganze (1969)

nodes.author: foucault
nodes.context: Foucault's inaugural lecture at the Collège de France. In every society, he argues, the production of discourse is controlled, selected and redistributed by procedures that ward off its powers and dangers.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Who may speak, about what, and when, is itself an order.
nodes.sourceLabel: Michel Foucault, L'Ordre du discours (Paris: Gallimard, 1971) [inaugural lecture, Collège de France, 2 Dec 1970]

nodes.author: dijkstra
nodes.work: On the Foolishness of 'Natural Language Programming'
nodes.context: Formal texts, he argues, need only satisfy a few simple rules to be manipulated legitimately, and that makes them an amazingly effective tool for ruling out the nonsense our native tongues make almost impossible to avoid.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Programming in natural language would be a regression, not progress. Written in the 1970s, it reads differently in the age of language models.
nodes.orig: Instead of regarding the obligation to use formal symbols as a burden, we should regard the convenience of using them as a privilege…
nodes.sourceLabel: EWD 667, UT Austin

nodes.author: dijkstra
nodes.work: How Do We Tell Truths That Might Hurt?
nodes.context: The same short memo says that the use of COBOL cripples the mind.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Whorf's hypothesis, applied to programming languages.
nodes.orig: The tools we use have a profound (and devious!) influence on our thinking habits, and, therefore, on our thinking abilities.
nodes.sourceLabel: EWD 498, UT Austin

nodes.author: annie-hall
nodes.context: In a cinema line, a man lectures loudly about McLuhan. Alvy Singer produces McLuhan himself from behind a display stand, and McLuhan tells the man he has it all wrong.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The theorist of media appears inside a medium to correct his own interpreter. It is Phaedrus 275e reversed: for once, the father arrives to help his text.
nodes.orig: You know nothing of my work.
nodes.sourceLabel: Annie Hall, dir. Woody Allen (United Artists, released 20 April 1977), cinema-queue scene with Marshall McLuhan cameo

nodes.author: backus
nodes.work: Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style?
nodes.context: Backus argues that languages modeled on the machine inherit its "von Neumann bottleneck," a word-at-a-time traffic of words through a narrow channel.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: He proposes an algebra of programs, where programs are combined like expressions and reasoned about like equations.
nodes.orig: Conventional programming languages are growing ever more enormous, but not stronger.
nodes.sourceLabel: ACM Digital Library

nodes.author: philip-k-dick
nodes.work: How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later
nodes.context: A 1978 speech on fake realities. If you control what words mean, he continues, you control the people who must use them.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Words are the lever by which reality is manipulated.
nodes.orig: Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away.
nodes.sourceLabel: Philip K. Dick, "How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later" (1978), in The Shifting Realities of Philip K. Dick, ed. Lawrence Sutin (Vintage, 1995)

nodes.author: philip-k-dick
nodes.context: The appendix is a numbered sequence of 52 aphorisms, modeled on the Tractatus.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: The Logos[divine Word, reason] is living information that enters human beings, and the world is information mistaken for objects.
nodes.orig: The Empire never ended.

nodes.author: ong
nodes.work: Orality and Literacy: The Technologizing of the Word
nodes.context: Ong, who studied under McLuhan at Saint Louis, contrasts primary oral cultures, which have never known writing, with literate ones. Chapter 4 is titled "Writing restructures consciousness."
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Writing is a technology, not a neutral record. It separates the knower from the known and makes lists, definitions, and analysis possible, which oral memory could not sustain. A grammar written down is a different thing from a grammar spoken.
nodes.orig: Writing restructures consciousness.
nodes.sourceLabel: Walter J. Ong, Orality and Literacy: The Technologizing of the Word (London: Methuen, 1982; 30th anniv. ed., Routledge, 2012), ch. 4 'Writing restructures consciousness'

nodes.author: postman
nodes.context: Postman sets Orwell's nightmare, in which books are banned, beside Huxley's, in which no one wants to read them, and argues that television has delivered Huxley's.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: His chapter title revises McLuhan: a medium does not just carry content, it imposes a way of defining truth. Public discourse conducted on television becomes entertainment, whatever its subject.
nodes.orig: The medium is the metaphor.
nodes.sourceLabel: Neil Postman, Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business (New York: Viking, 1985), ch. 1 'The Medium Is the Metaphor'

nodes.author: naur
nodes.context: The theory lives in the programmers, not in the text, so it cannot be fully written down. A program whose team has dispersed is, in Naur's term, dead, even if the code still runs, and reviving it means rebuilding the theory, not just reading the source.
nodes.interp: Placeholder: Plato's Phaedrus on writing, restated for software.
nodes.orig: …programming properly should be regarded as an activity by which the programmers form or achieve a certain kind of insight, a theory, of the matters at hand.
nodes.sourceLabel: Peter Naur, 'Programming as Theory Building', Microprocessing and Microprogramming 15, no. 5 (1985): 253–261; repr. in Naur, Computing: A Human Activity (ACM Press, 1992), 37–48

entry:anaximander-dk12-b1.author: anaximander
entry:anaximander-dk12-b1.date_note: approximate floruit; preserved by Simplicius (6th c. CE)

place.name: Miletus
place.why: Anaximander lived and taught in Miletus

entry:anaximander-dk12-b1.context: The oldest surviving sentence of Western philosophy, quoted by Simplicius, who notes that Anaximander says this "in rather poetic terms."

quotes.orig: ἐξ ὧν δὲ ἡ γένεσίς ἐστι τοῖς οὖσι, καὶ τὴν φθορὰν εἰς ταῦτα γίνεσθαι κατὰ τὸ χρεών· διδόναι γὰρ αὐτὰ δίκην καὶ τίσιν ἀλλήλοις τῆς ἀδικίας κατὰ τὴν τοῦ χρόνου τάξιν.
quotes.translit: ex hōn de hē genesis esti tois ousi, kai tēn phthoran eis tauta ginesthai kata to chreōn; didonai gar auta dikēn kai tisin allēlois tēs adikias kata tēn tou chronou taxin.
quotes.trans: From what things have their coming-to-be, into that they also pass away, according to necessity; for they pay penalty and retribution to one another for their injustice, according to the ordering of time.

entry:turing-computing-machinery-1950.context: Turing opens by posing the question, then immediately sets it aside because the meanings of "machine" and "think" can't be settled, and replaces it with the imitation game, a test carried out entirely in typed language. He predicts that by the century's end people will speak of machines thinking without being contradicted.

quotes.orig: I propose to consider the question, "Can machines think?"
too meaningless to deserve discussion
the use of words and general educated opinion will have altered so much

entry:wittgenstein-investigations.author: wittgenstein

place.name: Cambridge
place.why: mostly Cambridge; opening sections drafted at Skjolden

entry:wittgenstein-investigations.context: Wittgenstein's later remarks, numbered sections and the former "Part II" (PPF = the former "Part II.").

quotes.orig:
§19 — …eine Sprache vorstellen heißt, sich eine Lebensform vorstellen.
§43 — Die Bedeutung eines Wortes ist sein Gebrauch in der Sprache.
§109 — Die Philosophie ist ein Kampf gegen die Verhexung unseres Verstandes durch die Mittel unserer Sprache.
PPF §327 — Wenn ein Löwe sprechen könnte, wir könnten ihn nicht verstehen.
quotes.trans: To imagine a language means to imagine a form of life… The meaning of a word is its use in the language… Philosophy is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of our language… If a lion could talk, we could not understand him.

entry:wittgenstein-investigations.interpretation: Placeholder: Meaning is use within a form of life; philosophy fights the spells language casts.

entry:wittgenstein-tractatus.author: wittgenstein
entry:wittgenstein-tractatus.date_note: completed summer 1918 at Hallein; published 1921, English 1922

place.name: Hallein, near Salzburg
place.why: final text finished on leave at his uncle's house

entry:wittgenstein-tractatus.context: Wittgenstein's numbered propositions on logic, world and language. Ogden's 1922 version of 7: "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent."

quotes.orig:
1 — Die Welt ist alles, was der Fall ist.
4.0031 — Alle Philosophie ist »Sprachkritik«.
5.6 — Die Grenzen meiner Sprache bedeuten die Grenzen meiner Welt.
5.62 — …daß die Welt meine Welt ist…
6.522 — Es gibt allerdings Unaussprechliches. Dies zeigt sich, es ist das Mystische.
6.54 — Er muß sozusagen die Leiter wegwerfen, nachdem er auf ihr hinaufgestiegen ist.
7 — Wovon man nicht sprechen kann, darüber muß man schweigen.
quotes.trans: The world is all that is the case… All philosophy is 'critique of language'… The limits of my language mean the limits of my world… the world is my world… There is indeed the inexpressible. This shows itself; it is the mystical… He must, so to speak, throw away the ladder after he has climbed up it… What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence

entry:wittgenstein-tractatus.interpretation: Placeholder: Language pictures the world up to a limit; beyond it lies what can only be shown, and the book itself is a ladder to throw away.

entry:xenophanes-dk21-b15-16.author: xenophanes

place.name: Magna Graecia (Elea?)
place.why: wandering Sicily and south Italy after leaving Colophon

entry:xenophanes-dk21-b15-16.context: Xenophanes mocks the human-shaped gods of Homer and Hesiod.

quotes.orig: ἀλλ᾽ εἰ χεῖρας ἔχον βόες ἵπποι τ᾽ ἠὲ λέοντες / ἢ γράψαι χείρεσσι καὶ ἔργα τελεῖν ἅπερ ἄνδρες, / ἵπποι μέν θ᾽ ἵπποισι, βόες δέ τε βουσὶν ὁμοίας / καί κε θεῶν ἰδέας ἔγραφον…
quotes.translit: all' ei cheiras echon boes hippoi t' ēe leontes / ē grapsai cheiressi kai erga telein haper andres, / hippoi men th' hippoisi, boes de te bousin homoias / kai ke theōn ideas egraphon…
quotes.trans: If oxen and horses and lions had hands, and could draw and make works as men do, horses would draw the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen…

quotes.orig: Αἰθίοπές τε θεοὺς σφετέρους σιμοὺς μέλανάς τε / Θρῇκές τε γλαυκοὺς καὶ πυρρούς φασι πέλεσθαι.
quotes.translit: Aithiopes te theous spheterous simous melanas te / Thrēikes te glaukous kai pyrrous phasi pelesthai.
quotes.trans: The Ethiopians say their gods are snub-nosed and black, the Thracians that theirs are blue-eyed and red-haired.

entry:xenophanes-dk21-b15-16.interpretation: Placeholder: We make gods in our own image, and name them in our own words.
